Introduction to Quarto for Reproducibility
Lead: Steffi LaZerte
Length: 2-2.5 hours
Time: 2026-10-05 15:30 UTC

Description
Do you struggle to keep track of your research analyses in R? Is future-self constantly complaining about past-self’s inability to document scripts, data, and package versions? Come explore the magic of Quarto! Turn your R scripts into reproducible reports complete with all the information future-self needs to write up your analyses.
In this workshop we’ll learn about Markdown, RMarkdown and Quarto. We’ll cover different ways of creating reports from scripts and how to customize the output to maximize beauty as well as reproducibility. You will have the opportunity to learn and practice, and will go home with a collection of resources to help you along your journey. Example scripts to work with will be available, but best is to bring your own. Note that while the focus of this workshop is on R, Quarto also works with Python, so feel free to bring Python scripts to play with as well.
Participants do not need to be R experts but should be somewhat familiar with R and an R IDE (e.g., RStudio or Positron). Instructions for installing these programs will be sent out before the workshop.


Target audience
Anyone who has a passing familiarity with R/Python and who would like to learn more about creating reproducible reports of their analyses.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some familiarity with R and an R IDE (e.g., RStudio or Positron). Basic familiarity with R or Python is recommended.

text:
Introduction to stable-isotope assignment in R
Lead: Jackson Kusack
Length: 2-2.5 hours
Time: 2026-10-05 15:30 UTC

Description
For migratory wildlife populations, understanding the connections between breeding, non-breeding, and stopover locations is integral to their conservation and management. Intrinsic markers, such as stable isotopes, found within the tissues of migratory individuals offer an alternative to the use of transmitters and other extrinsic markers. Briefly, this method relates the stable-isotope values of consumer tissues to those of the environment (especially stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in precipitation) to determine likely origins where tissues were grown. In recent years there has been a handful of helpful packages released in the R statistical environment (isocat and AssignR) which have increased the functionality of these assignment methods and made them much more accessible.
In this workshop, I will first present a short introduction to the theory behind stable-isotope assignment, after which we will work through an example R script where we will, step-by-step, work though the procedures to determine the likely origins of unknown-origin migrants. No data is required by participants as everything will be provided during the workshop, but participants are welcome to apply the code to their own data.
The expected outcome for this workshop is that participants will gain a better understanding for the general approach and theory behind stable-isotope assignment using hydrogen isotopes and leave with some fundamental R code to build upon for their own analyses.


Target audience
Researchers and students who are interested in or are planning to collect tissues for stable isotope assignment. This workshop is aimed at a general audience.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some familiarity with R/Rmarkdown is suggested.

text:
Modeling Breeding Bird Survey with bbsBayes2: status, trends, and causal modeling of drivers of trends
Lead: Adam Smith
Length: 2-2.5 hours
Time: 2026-10-05 18:00 UTC

Description
bbsBayes2 is an R-package that allows for easy access to the North American Breeding Bird Survey data and for fitting a selection of hierarchical Bayesian models that estimate status and trends and can be modified to estimate the influence of spatial and temporal predictors on trends and abundance (e.g., Mckellar et al. 2025 and Smith et al. 2024). The package provides efficient, fully-Bayesian parameter estimation using Stan, spatially explicit models well suited to exploring spatial patterns in trends, and options to customize models to include covariates of trends and abundance. The package also allows for a streamlined Bayesian workflow that facilitates convergence diagnostics, prior and posterior predictions, visualization of model predictions, as well as cross-validation and model comparisons.
During this workshop you will follow along with live coding to get hands-on experience manipulating and visualizing output from a range of models and species. We will demonstrate the package’s functions, including those that allow you to:

Prepare the data for modeling a given species and fit a model that estimates trends for any time period (1970-2019, 2005-2015, 1980-2000, etc.).

Generate heat maps of population trends and graph population trajectories.

Choose from a suite of built-in hierarchical Bayesian models and access tools to help with cross-validation and model comparison.

Estimate trends for customized regions (e.g., all of the eastern Boreal, Great Plains versus eastern populations of grassland birds).

Build and fit customized models: the workshop allows plenty of time to explore customizing the base-models with examples of models that estimate regional climate-effects on population trends, local landcover effects on mean abundance, landcover change effects on trends, etc.



Target audience
Researchers and students interested in:

modeling spatial and temporal patterns in bird population over the last 60 years;

modeling covariates or causal drivers of variations in abundance and trends;

gaining experience in Bayesian workflow and fitting models using Stan;

better understanding the models used by the Canadian Wildlife Service, and the United States Geological Survey to estimate status and trends from BBS data.



Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Familiarity with coding in R is necessary. No prior experience with Stan or Bayesian models is required.

title: Workshops
section: Regulating incidental take in Canada: challenges and opportunities for scientists
text:
Regulating incidental take in Canada: challenges and opportunities for scientists
Lead: Julie Bourque
Length: 2-2.5 hours
Time: 2026-10-05 15:30 UTC

Description
Despite the federal prohibition on killing migratory birds and destroying their nests, approximately 269 million birds are killed and almost one million nests are destroyed annually in Canada due to otherwise lawful human activities. Bird mortality results from window collisions, fisheries bycatch, powerline electrocution, among other causes. Nest destruction is primarily associated with vegetation management activities during the breeding season including both temporary activities such as agriculture or forestry and permanent land conversion such as urbanization. This unintentional (incidental) take includes almost all spheres of human activities, both industrial and non-industrial, and is expected to increase as human development accelerates.
In the last few years, there has been renewed interest in regulating incidental take at the federal level. A regulatory system could provide benefits to migratory birds through the universal adoption of beneficial management practices in exchange for more legal certainty. However, such an initiative requires a strong scientific foundation to ensure that decision-making achieves conservation goals. For example, understanding the scope and impact of an activity is essential for establishing a baseline against which mitigation measures can be evaluated. Further research is also needed to evaluate evidence-based mitigation measures and their applicability in the Canadian context.
This workshop will examine the concept of incidental take and will aim to foster discussion on how scientists can influence regulatory and policy development through their research. The workshop will include a presentation followed by an open discussion with participants. The expected outcome is that participants will gain a better understanding of how to present the results of their research to policymakers to better support policy development for migratory birds in Canada. The workshop may also help researchers incorporate incidental take considerations into their work and strengthen collaboration between scientists and policymakers.


Target audience
The target audience consists of researchers with an interest in policy-making and with knowledge on the effects of human activities on migratory birds.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some prior knowledge of the prohibitions of the Migratory Birds Convention Act and the Migratory Birds Regulations 2022 is useful.

text:
Using WildTrax to manage and process your birdsong recordings
Lead: Kevin Kelly
Length: Full day / 4-5 hours
Time: 2026-10-05 15:30 UTC

Description
WildTrax is a free online platform developed to remove the barrier of entry for researchers and managers to manage and process ARU recordings at any scale of research program. Developed to help users manage and process acoustic data from raw recordings through to being used in statistical analyses, WildTrax allows users to store raw data, metadata, and derived species data on a cloud system that can be shared by collaborators anywhere in the world. With standardized metadata formats, processing methods and report outputs, the data can be easily stored and shared between users.
In this workshop we’ll teach you how to upload and manage acoustic recordings; store and manage metadata such as survey locations, field site visits, and field equipment information; process the recordings to identify the species vocalizing in the recordings; create and manage projects to aggregate your data into collective reports; use the built in birdsong recognizers (BirdNET and HawkEars) to enhance your processing abilities; and publish, share and download the data contained on WildTrax.
The workshop is set-up to be interactive so that users can follow along on the WildTrax platform to perform the various steps being presented using their own data or example data provided by the facilitators to learn the various features and functions available in WildTrax.


Target audience
This workshop is meant to appeal to novice passive acoustic monitoring users (basic understanding of an ARU and spectrogram) to a more experienced researcher wanting to learn how WildTrax can help with their data storage and processing needs.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Basic understanding of passive acoustic recordings and spectrograms is helpful.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Least Flycatchers are the most common nesting species in the aspen-balsam forest of the Beaverhill Natural Area in central Alberta. In 2022 Myrthe Van Brempt et al found that Least Flycatchers produce more eggs and young than elsewhere, have very high nest success, and have the highest breeding density in North America. Subsequently, they determined a shift to earlier autumn migration. Recently, we determined that nests were surviving the winter and being reused by Least Flycatchers. This talk will discuss the frequency and timing of nest reuse, and apparent benefits and possible risks of this unusual behavior. Nest reuse does not appear to be implicated in shift to earlier migration.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Invasive predators are a major threat to native species on islands. Predator removal programs have been successfully implemented on many small islands to protect native species; however, the removal of invasive predators can have unforeseen negative effects on native species, mediated by other non-target invasive species. Identifying these indirect effects is important to maximize the effectiveness of predator removals. New Zealand is planning a country-wide predator removal program to conserve native species being threatened by invasive mammalian predators. However, predator removals are also expected to benefit invasive bird species that compete with native species. Life history data suggest the proliferation of invasive birds in response to island-wide predator removals, further endangering the native species. While previous localized predator removals in New Zealand suggested that the effects of invasive birds did not impact the success of predator removals for native birds, we found that on an island-wide scale, these effects are likely to be important. We tested for indirect effects from invasive birds on native birds using simulations that incorporated life-history and spatially explicit data, which allowed us to simulate the effects of different treatments on populations in a landscape. Our results suggest that island-wide predator removals will benefit native bird populations, but that these benefits are diminished by indirect effects mediated by invasive birds. Thus, we suggest that New Zealand plan to incorporate strategies to mitigate effects from invasive birds so that the success of the predator removal will be maximized for native species. Our simulation provides a modelling tool for predicting indirect interactions in an ecosystem and has the potential to be used as an invasive species management tool in the future.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Vocal mimicry occurs across diverse bird families, yet its ecological and evolutionary significance remains poorly understood. Although there are many well-documented examples of mimicry in temperate-zone birds, we know remarkably little about vocal mimicry in the tropics. The genus Sporophila comprises 41 species of small, seed-eating finches known as “Seedeaters”. To date, vocal mimicry has been reported in seven of these 41 species. Given the lack of detailed studies of the South American avifauna, we can anticipate that mimicry is more widespread and that many examples remain to be described. To assess the extent of vocal mimicry in the Sporophila genus, we retrieved sound recordings from two major sound libraries. We scanned all high-quality recordings to assess the presence of vocal mimicry and the percentage of recordings containing mimicry for each species. We mapped vocal mimicry onto a Thraupidae family phylogenetic hypothesis made from a time-calibrated global avian phylogeny. We pruned the tree to include all species of the Sporophila genus and six outgroup species to calibrate the tree. Our results reveal that mimicry is more widespread than previously recognized in this genus, suggesting an important role of vocal mimicry in this poorly studied genus.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Elaborate bird songs are important for mate choice in many species. Song features may provide information about male parental behaviour or genetic quality. Using a field-based study of Savannah Sparrows in eastern Canada, we explored the relationship between male song and male parental behaviour. We measured male song rate and song structural features from audio recordings. We measured male provisioning rate from video recordings at nest sites. We found that male provisioning rate varied with song complexity: males who produced more introductory notes fed offspring less often. Given this relationship, we suggest that females may use male song to infer male parental behaviour when choosing a breeding partner. Upcoming genetic analysis of paternity will allow us to assess whether this relationship also influences genetic parentage. Investigating how male song features relate to parental care and female choice will improve our understanding of how reproductive behaviour is shaped by selection.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
As the need to monitor living species increases, traditional wildlife survey methods are often replaced by more efficient and less costly alternatives. Passive Acoustic Monitoring (hereafter PAM) has gained popularity in wildlife studies and is described as the gathering of acoustic data from sound-producing species virtually anywhere, at any time of day. Although this method offers crucial insights on wildlife ecology, PAM generates a large volume of data, which can be tedious since expertise and extensive effort are required to manually validate data. However, recent advances in bioacoustics allow scientists to pair PAM with audio-classification algorithms that are trained to recognize species-specific vocalizations, thereby reducing cost and resources needed. This benefits the monitoring of focal species with little-known ecology or cryptic behavior and helps expand the spatial and temporal footprint of species surveys. This is the case for the Bicknell’s thrush (Catharus bicknelli), an endangered boreal forest-dwelling bird in Canada. Most of its breeding territory is found in Québec’s highlands, at 800 m and above, in dense, regenerated balsam fir (Abies balsamea) stands. Since 2013, a mandatory survey of Bicknell’s thrush has been required to assess impact of future development projects on targeted habitat. As pressure on the species’ habitat is increasing, there is a need to adequately monitor and protect populations through more informed management mitigation measures. The main objective was to develop a standardized PAM methodology with audio-classification algorithms to efficiently process Bicknell’s thrush acoustic data on breeding grounds. The use of resulting protocol and recommendations is intended to standardize impact-assessment methods across Québec on one of the most elusive bird species in Canada. We surveyed Bicknell’s thrush in known breeding sites over four years to test and evaluate the performance of our proposed methods with different open-source algorithms.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Blackpoll Warblers (Setophaga striata; blackpolls) are one of the fastest declining passerines in North America. We lack clarity on which conservation issues are responsible for their documented decline of 92% in the past 50 years. The crosswise long-distance migration pattern of blackpolls is unique among neotropical migrants. From migration theory, we should expect that populations with longer migrations will face higher mortality rates. However, recent research has discovered the opposite. Eastern breeding blackpoll populations migrate the shortest distance and are declining significantly faster than western populations. Here, I extend what we know about blackpoll migration by using the Motus network to determine what habitat blackpolls are using during their southward migration. As part of long-term research on a collaborative research team, Motus tags are being deployed on blackpolls in Alaska, Manitoba, Québec, and Newfoundland. I will present an assessment of migration habitat quality that uses remote sensing data to quantify habitat characteristics surrounding Motus towers that blackpolls from each population pass by during their post-breeding migrations south. Future work will assess how apparent annual survival is correlated with different paces of migration, migration habitat quality, and wintering location from across the blackpoll range. Insights from this research will support regionally targeted conservation actions to improve outcomes for this rapidly declining songbird.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Forster’s Tern (Sterna forsteri) is an understudied North American waterbird with an indeterminate population status in potential decline. Compared to other North American Tern species, Forster’s Terns have shorter migrations, staying within North America throughout the annual cycle. The core of the Forster’s Tern breeding range is in interior wetlands of the Prairie Pothole Region, with additional breeding populations ranging across the southern Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts of the United States. My research aims to improve our knowledge of Forster’s Tern population structure and movement across the full annual cycle, including determining whether different subspecies exist, as was proposed more than 80 years ago. For this, I have two objectives: 1) assess population trends in relation to environmental covariates with the use of Citizen Science and remotely sensed environmental data, and 2) analyze population structure with the use of a combination of morphological and genetic data collected across their breeding populations. These analyses together will allow for a more complete understanding of Forster’s Terns, providing insight into their population status and structure across the annual cycle and helping determine whether separate populations should be treated as separate “Designatable Units” for the most optimal conservation and management strategies for the species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Urban development continues to replace natural landscapes as human populations grow, and urban landscapes are a matrix of novel resources and threats to birds. Cities are often built along migratory routes and migrating birds are further attracted to these regions by artificial light at night. Previous research has demonstrated that migrating songbirds commonly stopover in or near cities, yet there is limited information on their fine-scale habitat use during stopovers in urban green spaces. Conserving and managing these spaces is critical to provide habitat for birds during this energetically stressful period of their annual cycle. Our overall objective is to quantify stopover duration, habitat use, and diet selection of boreal-breeding passerines in a 108-ha multi-use urban park in Montreal, Canada by tagging, radio-tracking, and collecting fecal samples from birds during the post-breeding migratory period. Preliminary results from a pilot season at this park suggest that stopover lengths (9.6 ± 7.3 days, n=24) and temporary home range sizes (9.05 ± 8.75 -ha; 95% KDE, n=9) are highly variable among our eight focal species. Future analyses will include resource selection functions to quantify fine-scale habitat use and fecal DNA metabarcoding to compare diets of birds at the urban park with a nearby peri-urban site. This work is done in collaboration with local municipal land managers with the goal of providing advice on urban green space management for migratory bird conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Animals face uncertainty in every aspect of their lives. Where is the best territory? Who is the best available mate? When and where will food be available? To mitigate this uncertainty, one strategy organisms can adopt is to ‘sample’; updating their information about the state of territories, mates, and/or resources within their environment. Optimal sampling models ask: what sampling strategy should individuals adopt to maximize their fitness? In a foraging context, we can imagine an individual that encounters a patch that has recently become unprofitable. This individual must then decide how it should behave amidst this uncertainty in food availability. Should it revisit (i.e., sample) this patch later to see if the patch becomes profitable, or should it visit an alternative food patch? If an individual samples the previously encountered unprofitable patch, and the patch remains unprofitable, the individual suffers from sampling error costs. If an individual instead visits an alternative patch, but the initially unprofitable patch is now profitable, the individual misses out on exploiting this now profitable patch and experiences missed opportunity costs. Theory predicts that both sampling error and missed opportunity costs will influence individual sampling frequency. We tested these predictions using feeder visit data from a free-living winter population of black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus). We assessed how chickadee sampling frequency at empty feeders changed as a function of several variables predicted a priori to affect sampling error and/or missed opportunity costs. We found that although some factors influenced sampling frequency as predicted by optimal sampling theory, others did not. I discuss these results and propose explanations for how individual differences in sampling behaviour may influence fitness in our chickadee population.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Climate warming is driving the expansion of woody shrubs across the Arctic tundra, reshaping habitats critical to over 200 bird species. Shrub expansion is already altering avian ranges, behaviours, and population dynamics, yet the magnitude of these effects and the diversity of species affected remain unclear. We examined whether the breeding bird community on Qikiqtaruk–Herschel Island, Yukon, has changed over the past 37 years and whether these changes are associated with increasing tundra greenness. Using 37 years (1990–2026) of annual June breeding bird surveys conducted by Yukon Parks, we tested for long-term changes in community composition using multivariate statistical analyses. We found that the tundra bird community composition shifted significantly and was largely driven by species turnover. Species richness and Shannon diversity exhibited small but significant positive trends over the study period. Several shrub-associated species such as American Tree Sparrow (Spizelloides arborea) and Bluethroat (Luscinia svecica) have increased, while many open-tundra-nesting species like Baird’s Sandpiper (Calidris bairdii) and Lapland Longspur (Calcarius lapponicus) have decreased. Environmental vector fitting identified maximum annual NDVI, a proxy for tundra greenness that reflects vegetation change such as shrub expansion, as the strongest predictor of these compositional shifts. These findings support the hypothesis that climate-driven vegetation change is contributing to the long-term restructuring of tundra bird communities, with potential consequences for the persistence of open-tundra specialist species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) winter habitat is typically delineated from where birds are found, treating occupancy as a single outcome rather than the product of nested decisions made at different scales. We decomposed overwintering into its components: when birds departed, where they could have settled, where they did settle, and what they used once settled. We tracked 43 greater sage-grouse in northeastern Wyoming from 2017 – 2022, defining each individual’s departure-to-settlement transition from net squared displacement changepoints rather than fixed calendar dates. Realized winter ranges were compared against potential ranges along each bird’s own trajectory, then against the broader study area (second order), and GPS fixes against availability within each bird’s range (third order), with collinear covariates screened a priori and candidate models ranked by AICc with k-fold cross-validation. Winter range placement was best explained by eastness, terrain ruggedness, topographic position, vegetation height, and sagebrush cover. Where greater sage-grouse avoided rugged terrain and selected for areas with higher vegetation cover and height (e.g., sagebrush and shrubs). Selection for taller, denser sagebrush at the scale of range placement suggests birds commit to areas where shrub structure is likely to remain exposed above snowpack across an entire winter, rather than locating such cover opportunistically once settled. Avoidance of rugged terrain is consistent with both the energetic cost of movement through snow and the tendency of broken terrain to accumulate drifts.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Habitat loss and fragmentation are primary drivers of forest degradation and biodiversity decline, but disentangling their effects is challenging because they co-occur, may interact, and are perceived differently by different species, requiring species-specific definitions and explicit tests for additive and interactive effects. To quantify the effects of these processes on Black-throated Green Warblers (BTNW), a species of conservation concern in Alberta, we developed species-specific definitions of BTNW habitat (80–140 year old mixedwood forest) and fragmentation (edge density). We compared spatial occupancy models with habitat amount only, edge density only, and their additive and interactive effects using three increasingly comprehensive definitions of fragmentation (large polygonal disturbances only; adding wide linear features >8 m; and all anthropogenic disturbances including narrow 2–8 m seismic lines), at three spatial scales (7, 78, and 314 ha). The most comprehensive definition, including seismic lines, provided the best model fit at the 7 and 78 ha scales, indicating BTNW perceive even narrow disturbances as habitat boundaries. Edge density negatively affected occupancy at the two finer scales, but habitat amount became the dominant predictor at the broader 314 ha scale. Our species-specific approach revealed responses that generic classifications would likely obscure, demonstrating that conservation strategies for this species must consider spatial configuration alongside habitat amount. Given the strong negative effects of edge density and major population declines reported for BTNW in Alberta, we urge managers to minimize cumulative edge creation through harvest planning and active seismic line regeneration.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Aggressive behaviours, including alarm calling and predator mobbing, are frequently used by nesting birds to deter predators and improve reproductive success. These behaviours also provide opportunities for nearby nesting birds of other species to eavesdrop and glean information about predator threats, thereby reducing their nest predation risk. In the subarctic, whimbrels (Numenius spp.) frequently engage in aggressive alarm calling that may reduce nest predation risk and improve reproductive success of nearby nesting shorebirds. This has been suggested in Europe between Bar-tailed Godwits (Limosa lapponica) and Eurasian Whimbrels (N. phaeopus), where godwits choose their nest sites after whimbrels do and place them closer to whimbrels than expected by chance, possibly for protection. However, the influence of whimbrels on the incubation behaviour of nearby shorebirds has not been documented. Furthermore, nesting associations remain unexplored for other whimbrel species, such as the Hudsonian Whimbrel (N. hudsonicus) in North America. My research tests whether Hudsonian Whimbrel alarm calls affect the incubation behaviours of two co-occurring shorebirds, Short-billed Dowitchers (Limnodromus griseus) and Dunlins (Calidris alpina) in fen ecosystems near Churchill, Manitoba. To do so, I video-recorded incubating individuals during playback experiments featuring a randomized sequence of: 1) Hudsonian Whimbrel alarm calls, 2) Short-billed Dowitcher alarm calls, 3) Dunlin alarm calls, and 4) a sympatric frog chorus control (Boreal Chorus Frog, Pseudacris maculata; and Wood Frog, Lithobates sylvaticus), each separated by a 10-minute latency period. Fieldwork occurred in the summer of 2026, with results to be presented. As Hudsonian Whimbrels rapidly decline, this study may demonstrate their importance in shaping shorebird antipredator strategies and nest success in the Canadian subarctic. Doing so would provide justification to uplist their conservation status, consequently benefitting their entire shorebird nesting community.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Birds are a vital component of urban biodiversity worldwide, yet accurately measuring their abundance and diversity is challenging because most survey methods are not designed for dense urban environments. Surveys are often limited to green spaces, wealthier neighborhoods and high-income countries, hindering our understanding of how birds use all urban habitats. We developed and evaluated the Global Urban Bird Survey, an inclusive method for surveying urban birds across diverse city environments. Local experts trained and coordinated community members, who conducted repeated surveys using acoustic monitors in five cities between 2022 and 2024: Dakar, Nairobi, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, and Toronto. Survey locations were selected via a stratified block-randomized design within city cores, ensuring unbiased coverage across habitats. We compared the performance of the Global Urban Bird Survey with eBird, a widely used community science platform, to assess species richness, occurrence, and spatial coverage. eBird detected significantly higher mean species richness than the Global Urban Bird Survey in Dakar, Nairobi, Paris, and Rio de Janeiro, while no significant difference was observed in Toronto. However, eBird’s spatial coverage was substantially lower than that of the Global Urban Bird Survey, particularly in low-income cities. The Global Urban Bird Survey provides a robust, scalable approach to monitoring urban avian biodiversity across a range of habitats and socioeconomic contexts. Broader, more representative sampling of urban environments is critical for understanding global patterns of biodiversity. Community-based acoustic monitoring complements existing citizen science efforts, offering a tool for inclusive conservation planning and informed urban biodiversity management worldwide

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Small parids like black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) rely on caching (i.e. storing food for later use) as a strategy to mitigate starvation risk during winter. Although caching can occur throughout the autumn and winter, it is predicted that most intense period should occur in late summer/early fall, when natural food availability is high, daylength is long, and ambient temperatures are favourable to both meet immediate energetic needs and invest in building up caches. Quantifying caching in free-living birds is time consuming, and thus, relatively few studies have quantified seasonal peaks in caching. Here, we assess if feeders can be used to capture seasonal peaks in caching investment using automated detections of black-capped chickadees fitted with passive integrated transponders to quantify caching in late summer -early fall. From previous studies and theoretical calculations, the number of sunflower seeds required to meet daily energetic requirements at this time of year is estimated to be ~45 seeds, and thus, daily feeder visits in excess of 45 can be inferred to indicate caching. We tested theoretical predictions about seasonal caching peaks, the effect of temperature and differences between sexes. We found that both day in season and temperature play important roles in shaping seasonal caching patterns as predicted, but contrary to theoretical predictions, females invested less in caching than males. Further, the observed seasonal peak in caching using feeders was much shorter compared caching peaks in populations without supplemental food. Our findings demonstrate that feeder-based studies can capture biologically meaningful variation in caching behaviour, with some important caveats, and highlight the combined influence of seasonal and short-term energetic factors on food-caching strategies.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Freshwater ecosystems are increasingly threatened by contamination from toxic elements such as arsenic, manganese and lead, largely driven by mining, industrial discharge and agricultural activities. These pollutants can persist in aquatic environments, accumulating in sediments and entering food webs, where they pose risks to aquatic organisms and higher trophic levels. In river systems such as the Deka and Lukosi, which are influenced by anthropogenic activities, there is growing concern about the extent of contamination and its ecological implications.
Aquatic organisms, particularly fish, play a critical role in transferring contaminants through trophic interactions, while predatory aquatic birds may serve as effective bioindicators of environmental pollution due to their position at the top of the foodweb. Despite this, limited information exists on the distribution and bioaccumulation of toxic elements within these river systems and their potential magnification across trophic levels.
This study aims to investigate the concentrations of arsenic, manganese and lead in water, sediment and fish within the Deka and Lukosi rivers, and to assess their subsequent bioaccumulation in predatory aquatic birds. We hypothesize that contaminant levels will vary spatially and that bioaccumulation will increase with trophic position, reflecting biomagnification processes.
By linking environmental contamination to biological uptake across multiple trophic levels, this research seeks to provide insight into ecosystem health and the potential risks posed to aquatic biodiversity and avian species, while informing future monitoring and conservation strategies.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Inbreeding is the mating of two closely related individuals. Inbred offspring are more likely to receive multiple copies of the same alleles. This may lead to the expression of recessive alleles, and reductions in success. Studies of many wild bird species have shown that inbreeding can lead to decreased fitness. Pukeko are noteworthy in that they regularly engage in inbreeding in parts of their range, despite the expected fitness consequences. They are also unique in that they engage in joint-laying; a breeding system with multiple females laying eggs in a shared nest. As such, we expect that each clutch will contain some eggs that are from consanguineous pairings, and some that are not. Our study aimed to explore the consequences of inbreeding in this species. We hypothesized that we would see decreased success of inbred chicks compared to outbred ones and therefore predicted that inbred chicks would fail to hatch more often when compared to outbred ones. We performed breeding bird surveys in Tawharanui Regional Park, Auckland, New Zealand where they are known to inbreed. Once we identified breeding groups and their nests, we collected blood samples from all chicks that hatched, and tissue samples from all eggs with a developed embryo that failed to hatch. We extracted DNA from samples, then genotyped all chicks using established microsatellites for the species to calculate inbreeding coefficients. We used a generalized mixed model to determine whether inbreeding coefficient impacted the probability that a chick will hatch. We found that inbred chicks were less likely to hatch than their outbred nest mates. This shows that there are decreases in fitness that occur from the frequent inbreeding, in spite of which the Pukeko persist. This warrants future work to study other aspects of their inbreeding, and whether inbreeding impacts their fitness in other ways.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Forest management practices designed to reduce the impacts of logging on wildlife may not always provide the habitat conditions necessary for successful reproduction. In some cases, retained habitat may continue to attract breeding individuals while failing to support reproductive success, potentially creating ecological traps. For the federally Endangered Williamson’s Sapsucker (Sphyrapicus thyroideus), forestry best management practices (BMPs) have been developed for use in British Columbia. However, these voluntary practices are applied only within the species’ known area of occupancy, and their effectiveness in supporting successful reproduction has never been evaluated. To determine whether current forestry BMPs provide habitat that supports successful reproduction, we are linking nest productivity to habitat characteristics, focusing on nesting and foraging conditions in both managed and unmanaged forests. During the 2025 and 2026 breeding seasons, occupancy surveys were conducted throughout the Princeton and Boundary regions of southern British Columbia to locate breeding territories and active nest cavities. Nest productivity was monitored using repeated visual observations, custom-built cavity cameras, and acoustic recording units to document clutch size, hatching success, fledging success, and nest failure. Habitat assessments quantified nest-tree characteristics, stand structure, and surrounding forest composition across protected forests, retention-harvested stands, and unlogged forests. This project will provide the first direct evaluation of whether current forestry BMPs support the successful reproduction of Williamson’s Sapsucker in Canada. By identifying the nesting and foraging habitat characteristics associated with nest success and failure, the results will help guide future refinements to forestry BMPs and inform recovery planning and long-term conservation of this Endangered species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Volunteer science is foundational to long-term avian monitoring; yet, without clear understanding of volunteer characteristics, complex strategies to model observer effects remain a necessary but compromised avenue for advancing ornithological research. I address this by investigating how observer characteristics are navigated across the data lifecycle. My previous research 1) quantified influence of observer characteristics on population trend estimates, and 2) found that 51% of uses of Canadian volunteer-contributed bird data in the peer-reviewed literature do not explicitly address the volunteer nature of the data. This study examines the perspectives of experts across stages of the data lifecycle, using interviews and reflexive thematic analysis to identify practical and epistemic constraints shaping how observer characteristics are operationalized in practice. Situating these effects within real-world data management constraints informs methodological improvements and transparent reporting standards in ornithological research. This presentation will discuss potential explanations for the lack of transparency identified in the literature, the diversity of approaches used across programs to ensure reliable data from planning stages through to end-use, and what experts might do differently given unlimited resources. These findings will help bridge the gap between statistical methods for addressing observer variation and their practical application in ornithology, supporting appropriate and respectful use of volunteer-contributed bird data for evidence-based conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Community science methods have the capacity to expand our knowledge of biodiversity by bridging barriers to research in economically marginalized regions, both globally and locally. The Global Urban Bird Survey (GUBS) collected audio and video recordings at randomized survey points distributed across the urban core of five cities around the world, including Dakar, Senegal. Although many studies have evaluated biodiversity in cities, primarily urban greenspaces, GUBS provides a more representative sample of avian species richness across all habitats in a city, providing important data on biodiversity in economically disadvantaged an underrepresented areas. We used the GUBS data from Dakar to assess relationships between green ground cover, human activity levels, and avian species richness, gauging the potential of using low-tech community science methods for these analyses. In addition to previously completed acoustic analysis to identify species richness at each survey point, we enlisted community members to rank green ground cover and human activity levels in 35 videos across the city of Dakar. We found that increased green ground cover and decreased human activity levels were associated with increased avian species richness. These preliminary findings provide evidence that predictors of bird biodiversity in Dakar city hold consistent patterns across diverse neighborhoods, even with the use of low-tech community science methods, paralleling previous evidence of positive effects of greenspace and negative effects of human activity on urban biodiversity. Given these findings, we are expanding the study to three of the other GUBS cities: Toronto (Canada), Nairobi (Kenya), and Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), to determine if the relationships we found in Dakar are consistent across these diverse cities. Overall, this study demonstrates the utility of low-tech approaches to evaluate the effects of features of the urban landscape that might limit or support biodiversity in cities.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Arrival timing on breeding grounds is closely tied to reproductive success in migratory waterfowl. Better understanding of spring migration characteristics and carryover effects on annual productivity is needed to inform sustainable harvest management. Updated assessments of these population dynamics are notably important to guide harvest management decisions of the declining Southern Hudson Bay (SHB) population of Canada geese (Branta canadensis interior). Canada geese are the most harvested goose species across eastern North America, and SHB Canada geese are both culturally important and a key resource for subsistence hunters in Ontario’s northern communities. We investigated spring migration strategies of SHB Canada geese to assess how environmental conditions influence arrival timing and subsequent nesting success. From 2022–2025, we deployed 151 Ornitela GPS–GSM neck collar transmitters on adult breeding females, generating high-resolution movement data throughout the annual cycle. Using linear mixed effects models, we evaluated how snowmelt and temperature influence migration characteristics, and how those characteristics relate to nest success. Migration timing varied substantially among individuals, with arrivals to breeding areas ranging from mid-April to early May. Preliminary results indicate that regional snowmelt and temperature strongly influence the number and duration of migratory stopovers. Canada geese typically follow the snowline closely during spring migration, and some individuals arrived ahead of snowmelt and staged at lower latitudes until conditions improved. Importantly, later-arriving individuals exhibited lower nesting success, suggesting that delayed arrival may reduce reproductive performance. Our findings clarify spring migration strategies of the Southern Hudson Bay Population of Canada geese and highlight the importance of timely arrival for breeding success. Early arrival may benefit geese as spring phenology advances under climate change, yet mismatches between arrival timing and local environmental conditions could still affect productivity.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Birds in North America are facing steep population declines. This trend has been attributed to several anthropogenic factors, and climate change is at the forefront. Many multi-brooded species now breed earlier and have prolonged breeding seasons, extending into the hotter summer months. As a result, nestlings may face increased overheating, reductions in condition, and increased mortality. Temperature effects vary by geographic location, making localized studies necessary to understand impacts on species within a region. European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris), an urban-thriving passerine, are declining in North America. Starlings are double-brooded, with their breeding season occurring from April-July in eastern Canada. Using a wild, nest box breeding population of European Starlings in Halifax, Nova Scotia, we examined nestling condition and fledging success over two decades (2007-2026) and their relation to rising temperatures in our region. We predicted that nestling condition and fledging success would decrease over time as annual temperatures increase. We also predicted that late brood nestlings would be in poorer overall condition and have lower fledge success rates compared to those in early broods. Our long-term study will provide insight into how a bird species in Nova Scotia is responding to climate change.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Many migratory bird populations face ongoing declines, driven by various factors including anthropogenic threats such as cat predation, collisions, and pollution. The magnitude of their exposure to some of these threats in urban landscapes across their annual cycle remains poorly understood. We aim to quantify the urban exposure throughout the annual cycle of the urban-tolerant Yellow Warblers (Setophaga petechia) and more urban-avoidant Chestnut-sided Warblers (S. pensylvanica). We predict that a species’ association with urban areas on the breeding grounds is indicative of their exposure during the rest of the annual cycle. To test if Yellow Warblers may be more exposed to urban areas throughout the year, we deployed archival light-level geolocators on breeding birds (n=88), and radio tags on migrating individuals (n=73) in Quebec, Canada. Geolocators and radio tags revealed that Chestnut-sided warblers breeding in southern Quebec migrate along the Eastern coast and winter in Costa Rica and Nicaragua, while Yellow warblers migrate further west and winter in Colombia and Venezuela. We suggest that Chestnut-sided Warblers have the highest urban exposure during migration, and have a more urbanized migratory path than Yellow Warblers, which breed and winter in more anthropogenically disturbed sites than Chestnut-sided Warblers.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The population of LeConte’s sparrow (Ammospiza leconteii) is declining across the portion of its breeding range which falls in Western Canada. LeConte’s sparrow has been identified as a priority for conservation assessment and management by Canadian government agencies, but the species is poorly understood in terms of its ecology and distribution. We developed a high-resolution species distribution model (SDM) of LeConte’s sparrow occurrence in the Prairie Ecozone of Canada to investigate the habitat associations and spatial distribution of LeConte’s sparrow and identify candidate areas for land conservation. A maximum entropy (MaxEnt) method was used to predict the probability of occurrence for LeConte’s sparrow. In the presence observations dataset, 2,595 of 8,253 (31%) occurrences may have represented positional uncertainty as they were located on roads and in open bodies of water. As most SDMs rarely correct for fine-scale positional uncertainty, we tested three different correction distances (relocating observations to adjacent habitat). We compared three different models (no relocations; relocations within 30m; relocations within 100m) and found that they performed similarly. Covariates used to predict occurrence included proximity to wetlands, land use, elevation, mean summer precipitation, and a normalized difference vegetation index. Model performance and output was similar across corrections, and we selected the 100m correction to maximize sample size. Probability of occurrence for LeConte’s sparrow showed a strong association with low elevation prairie wetlands and riparian areas, including urban rivers. To develop recommendations for land conservation, we identified seven priority locations where existing protected areas could be expanded to include potential habitat for LeConte’s sparrow. We encourage managers to field-validate and apply our model to inform habitat protection for this species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Advanced Facility for Avian Research at Western University is a world class facility consisting of faculty and trainees that aim to understand how the environment shapes bird ecology. Researchers across disciplines use integrative approaches to investigate everything bird, from neurobiology and behaviour to migratory physiology and conservation. To showcase the innovative research possible at AFAR, we will present on the tools and facilities used to address a multitude of research questions, both ongoing and for the future. In addition to working toward a better understanding of bird biology and ecology, we are passionate about training the next generation of critical thinkers and scientists.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The boreal forest is a vast and remote biome covering much of northern Canada and Alaska, which provides habitat for a substantial portion of the nearctic avifauna. The remoteness of much of this region limited earlier systematic monitoring efforts that hampered the development of data-informed decision support tools to aid bird conservation in response to increasing anthropogenic pressures. The Boreal Avian Modelling project (BAM) was formed as a collaborative initiative in 2004 to address this gap by amalgamating, harmonizing and integrating disparate point count data to develop tools for boreal bird conservation. We provide an overview of BAM’s development, including the individual research groups that make up the collective BAM team, and highlight BAM’s keystone tools for bird conservation. We discuss evolving conservation challenges and opportunities of new technologies and open data initiatives that can enhance science-based conservation tools for boreal birds.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Birds Canada delivers strong science across the country and beyond through more than a dozen regional networks of employees, volunteers, and partners collaborating toward shared conservation goals. Our science is diverse involving many different research themes, core questions, methodologies, ecosystems, and focal species. Much of our science falls under two key initiatives: tracking the state of Canada’s birds and leveraging science to drive conservation. Our 50+ science staff members leverage data from volunteer scientists and conservation technologies (NatureCounts, Motus, WildTrax, and more) to answer timely questions of conservation interest, and we often partner with universities on graduate student projects. Ultimately all of our science helps generate the critical knowledge and evidence needed to catalyze actions that help birds and their habitats thrive. In this presentation, we give a top-down overview of science at Birds Canada, and describe a broad selection of examples of Birds Canada science in action.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Canadian Network of Avian Data (CanAvian) unites a broad community of researchers, conservation practitioners, and volunteer scientists who generate, manage, and share extensive biodiversity data needed for ecological research. CanAvian is governed by a Steering Committee, Advisory Committees, and Working Groups coordinating priorities across science, data management, and community engagement. CanAvian brings together three of Canada’s largest biodiversity data platforms: NatureCounts (380 million records), Motus (8 billion records), and WildTrax (16 million records), supporting over 4,500 scientific publications. Supported by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, CanAvian is establishing harmonized data access policies and interoperability standards to support FAIR and CARE principles and improve data sharing across platforms and data repositories. These connections will support increasingly integrated and large-scale analyses required by modern ecological research and Canada’s biodiversity commitments. CanAvian has open pathways for membership, data contribution, and data access and invites participation from across Canada’s ornithological community.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Drs Ann McKellar, Nancy Mahony, Greg Mitchell, and Elizabeth Gow are Research Scientists from Environment and Climate Change Canada’s Science and Technology Branch, Biodiversity Research Division, who study the conservation of migratory birds in working landscapes. Their research, which extends from the Canadian western forests and Prairies to Atlantic Canada, takes a full annual cycle approach to 1) examine effects of agriculture, forestry, and urbanization on avian distribution, abundance, and fitness, 2) assess population structure and migratory connectivity of priority species and species at risk, and 3) quantify threats associated with aerial and urban habitats. They aim to develop evidence-based solutions that support biodiversity, ecosystem goods and services, and human well-being in working landscapes. The team, including their graduate students, collaborates extensively with universities (where they are Adjunct professors), ENGOs, other federal departments, and governments, both nationally and internationally.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Institute for Wetland and Waterfowl Research (IWWR) at Ducks Unlimited Canada conducts interdisciplinary research that advances ornithology within the broader context of wetland ecosystems. Centered on waterfowl ecology, IWWR studies waterfowl habitat use, productivity, and population dynamics, with particular emphasis on breeding landscapes such as the Prairie Pothole Region, while extending across boreal and other wetland systems nationally. Beyond core ornithological questions, IWWR develops quantitative tools and models to guide conservation planning and evaluate program outcomes, ensuring that habitat investments are effective, adaptive, and evidence-based. This includes assessing when programs should be refined, scaled, or phased out. Complementing our work in waterfowl ecology, we have developed substantial research capacity in biodiversity, climate change, carbon dynamics, wetland biogeochemistry, and sustainable agriculture, reflecting emerging priorities in wetland conservation science. Together, these efforts integrate waterfowl science with broader ecological processes to support both understanding and adaptive, outcome-driven conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Based at the University of New Brunswick’s Saint John Campus, the Atlantic Laboratory for Avian Research is directed by seabird biologist Dr. Heather Major. The lab studies relationships between bird populations and environmental change in marine and island ecosystems. Species of interest include the Atlantic Puffin, Razorbill, Common Murre, Arctic Tern, and Leach’s Storm-petrel primarily studied on Machias Seal Island (MSI) in the Bay of Fundy. MSI has been the focal site for the labs’ long-term seabird monitoring project that has been operated annually since 1995. In addition, the lab is currently collaborating on a project assessing feasibility of an island restoration at Seal Island, NS by removing introduced species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Thompson Rivers University is in the southern interior of British Columbia on the ancestral lands of the Tk’emlúps te Secwépemc (Kamloops main campus) within Secwepemcúl̓ecw, the traditional and unceded territory of the Secwépemc. This vast area of grasslands, forests, mountains, rivers and lakes is larger than all but four European countries, stretching from Jasper to Revelstoke to Kamloops to north of Williams Lake. Its diverse landscapes provide a rich opportunity for research about the impact of accelerating environmental change on avian ecology and to partner with First Nations. This showcase will highlight core themes of research guided by a group of faculty members who collaboratively mentor graduate students on projects that include: conservation of grassland-dependent bird species; braiding Indigenous and Western knowledges to inform species conservation; responses of bird communities to urbanization, industrial activity, and wildfire; and community-engaged efforts to monitor avian population change.

text:
Early Career Research Award Plenary
From wingbeats to the twilight zone: how biologging has changed our perspective in marine ornithology
Allison Patterson, Allison.patterson@ec.gc.ca
Biodiversity Research Division, Environment and Climate Change Canada, Dartmouth, NS
As a seabird biologist, I have spent untold hours in a blind observing birds return to their nests to feed their young and wondered “Where did they get that fish?” Ornithologists are fascinated by watching birds interact with their environment and share a common experience of mild disappointment when the object of our attention inevitably flies out of sight. Biologging shifts the perspective of our measurements from the observer to the individual bird. The proliferation of biologging technologies over the last 25 years has revolutionized how we study birds, allowing ornithologists to observe individual bird movements over large spatio-temporal scales and at increasingly fine resolution. Marine ornithology was historically constrained by the inherent challenges of observing birds at sea. Advances in biologging represent a sea change for seabird research, creating opportunities to empirically investigate questions in ecology that were inconceivable to previous generations of scientists. I will present examples from my research – using wingbeat frequencies to measure foraging success, examining the energetics of foraging in the marine twilight zone by an Arctic seabird, and modelling year-round distributions of seabirds that migrate across the Atlantic Ocean – to discuss opportunities and challenges in using biologging to advance seabird ecology and support marine conservation.

title: Conference Guide
text:
A Beginner’s Guide to the SCO-SOC
Adapted from the “A Beginner’s Guide to SCO-SOC 2025”
Attending a conference can be intimidating, but don’t worry – the SCO-SOC beginner’s guide to conferencing is here to help! Browse this guide for things you can do before, during, and after the conference to give you the best possible experience.

title: Conference Guide
section: Before the Conference
text:
Before the Conference

Review the Code of Conduct
The SCO-SOC meeting should be a respectful, safe, and fun environment. Review the conference code of conduct so that you know what is expected of attendees and what to do if someone acts inappropriately.


Review the Program & Plan Connections
Consider people of interest you might like to connect with during the conference. Explore the program to see if they are presenting or perhaps members of their lab are and make a note to check out those events. You can attend the social events and keep an eye out for the opportunity to introduce yourself.


Practice Your Pitch
The SCO-SOC meeting is a place for people to learn who you are and what you do. Practice a 30-second description of yourself to use when you meet new people. It may also be useful to develop a few questions to help start a conversation when you meet someone new. An easy question to ask just about any one is whether they have anything exciting coming up, either professionally or personally.
Pro tip! If you find public speaking or networking intimidating, look for a local Toastmasters club to practice your impromptu speaking.


Review Your Online Presence
It’s hard to hand out business cards at an online conference, but one thing you can do is make sure your online presence is up-to-date. Check your professional spaces (personal website, lab website, LinkedIn, Research Gate, OrcID, Google Scholar, GitHub etc.) and make sure that at least your current position and email address are up-to-date. If you list a CV, perhaps give it a quick update as well. If you have public social media profiles related to your professional self (X, Bluesky, Mastodon, etc.) make sure they’re up-to-date. If you have public social media profiles related to your personal self (Facebook, Instagram, etc.), take a moment to review them. Do you want that information to be public or findable by someone searching your name after meeting you at the conference? Consider making social media associated with your personal life private.


Choose How You Want to Appear
Even at an online conference, wear clothes that make you feel comfortable and confident. There will be social events and opportunities to interact with other conference attendees online, so consider what you want to wear and what your space looks like behind your camera. Ensure you can speak freely if you wish to participate in networking or socializing. If you have clothing, accessories, or art that feature birds, that can also be a fun conversation starter! It doesn’t matter if people are in your background, or if you’re attending from home. But it does matter if that makes you uncomfortable. In that case consider using the option to fuzz your background or move your setup to a place which only shows things you don’t mind having on display. Finally, make sure you have comfy shoes and binoculars accessible for going outside during breaks and participating in the eBird Trip Report and the Scavenger hunt!
Pro tip! Look at these photos from AOS-SCO 2023 and SCO-SOC 2025 to see what people wore!


Prepare Your Space
Online conferences make it easy to multitask, but this also makes it hard to focus on the talks and events. However, it can be useful to be able to look up people, labs, or topics, or to take digital notes. If you have access to a second monitor, see if you can take advantage of that to have conference talks on one screen and a web browser/note taker on the other. Even having your phone or a table ready in addition to a laptop can help.

title: Conference Guide
section: During the Conference
text:
During the Conference

Limit Multitasking
Try to limit multitasking unrelated to the conference. Paying attention and being able to ask followup questions during the event or in later emails can be really useful if you’re interested in making a connection with the speaker or their lab, or finding opportunities for the future.


Monitor the Roost
Browse The Roost, the Birds Canada hosted online community for ornithologists. There will be an SCO-SOC 2026 category related to conference topics. Read what others are saying or contribute your own thoughts and questions.


Pace Yourself
While there will be a lot of fun things happening at the SCO-SOC meeting, even at online conferences it is important to take breaks and prioritize rest. Though some experienced conference-goers may relish every moment of a conference, others may find it draining to be constantly socializing and absorbing information, especially on the computer. Take breaks as needed, and feel free to skip or leave events early to get a better night’s sleep.


Make New Connections
It can be tricky to network at online conferences, so take advantage of the question periods and social events designed to facilitate networking and socializing. Interactions can be both formal, like asking people questions during the Q&A period, and informal, such as chatting during a social event. If you’re starting to consider future career steps (grad school, post-doc, applying for post-graduate jobs, etc.) making yourself ‘visible’ (asking questions, introducing yourself, etc.) and letting people know that you’re looking for opportunities can be a great help. You never know what might come down the line through word of mouth. It’s important to remember that you likely won’t “click” with everyone to whom you talk. If someone isn’t as engaged as you had hoped, don’t take it personally and keep trying to meet new people.

title: Conference Guide
section: After the Conference
text:
After the Conference

Follow Up with Connections
After taking a few days to recharge, contact the people you met at the SCO-SOC meeting. This will help you both remember what you discussed! You might reach out with a quick email, a LinkedIn request, or whatever works for you.


Thank Your Supporters
If people helped you prepare for the SCO-SOC meeting, send them a thank-you note to tell them about your conference experience. Not only does this show appreciation, but it also may make supporters more likely to help other students in the future.


Update Your Resume
Update your CV or resume to list the presentations you delivered and any awards you received at SCO-SOC. Doing this now may save you a headache next time you need to provide someone with your CV – you don’t want to forget details about what you did at the SCO-SOC meeting!

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
bbsBayes2 is an R-package that allows for easy access to the North American Breeding Bird Survey data and for fitting a selection of hierarchical Bayesian models that estimate status and trends and can be modified to estimate the influence of spatial and temporal predictors on trends and abundance (e.g., Mckellar et al. 2025 and Smith et al. 2024). The package provides efficient, fully-Bayesian parameter estimation using Stan, spatially explicit models well suited to exploring spatial patterns in trends, and options to customize models to include covariates of trends and abundance. The package also allows for a streamlined Bayesian workflow that facilitates convergence diagnostics, prior and posterior predictions, visualization of model predictions, as well as cross-validation and model comparisons.
During this workshop you will follow along with live coding to get hands-on experience manipulating and visualizing output from a range of models and species. We will demonstrate the package’s functions, including those that allow you to:

Prepare the data for modeling a given species and fit a model that estimates trends for any time period (1970-2019, 2005-2015, 1980-2000, etc.).

Generate heat maps of population trends and graph population trajectories.

Choose from a suite of built-in hierarchical Bayesian models and access tools to help with cross-validation and model comparison.

Estimate trends for customized regions (e.g., all of the eastern Boreal, Great Plains versus eastern populations of grassland birds).

Build and fit customized models: the workshop allows plenty of time to explore customizing the base-models with examples of models that estimate regional climate-effects on population trends, local landcover effects on mean abundance, landcover change effects on trends, etc.



Target audience
Researchers and students interested in:

modeling spatial and temporal patterns in bird population over the last 60 years;

modeling covariates or causal drivers of variations in abundance and trends;

gaining experience in Bayesian workflow and fitting models using Stan;

better understanding the models used by the Canadian Wildlife Service, and the United States Geological Survey to estimate status and trends from BBS data.



Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Familiarity with coding in R is necessary. No prior experience with Stan or Bayesian models is required.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
Do you struggle to keep track of your research analyses in R? Is future-self constantly complaining about past-self’s inability to document scripts, data, and package versions? Come explore the magic of Quarto! Turn your R scripts into reproducible reports complete with all the information future-self needs to write up your analyses.
In this workshop we’ll learn about Markdown, RMarkdown and Quarto. We’ll cover different ways of creating reports from scripts and how to customize the output to maximize beauty as well as reproducibility. You will have the opportunity to learn and practice, and will go home with a collection of resources to help you along your journey. Example scripts to work with will be available, but best is to bring your own. Note that while the focus of this workshop is on R, Quarto also works with Python, so feel free to bring Python scripts to play with as well.
Participants do not need to be R experts but should be somewhat familiar with R and an R IDE (e.g., RStudio or Positron). Instructions for installing these programs will be sent out before the workshop.


Target audience
Anyone who has a passing familiarity with R/Python and who would like to learn more about creating reproducible reports of their analyses.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some familiarity with R and an R IDE (e.g., RStudio or Positron). Basic familiarity with R or Python is recommended.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
For migratory wildlife populations, understanding the connections between breeding, non-breeding, and stopover locations is integral to their conservation and management. Intrinsic markers, such as stable isotopes, found within the tissues of migratory individuals offer an alternative to the use of transmitters and other extrinsic markers. Briefly, this method relates the stable-isotope values of consumer tissues to those of the environment (especially stable isotopes of hydrogen and oxygen in precipitation) to determine likely origins where tissues were grown. In recent years there has been a handful of helpful packages released in the R statistical environment (isocat and AssignR) which have increased the functionality of these assignment methods and made them much more accessible.
In this workshop, I will first present a short introduction to the theory behind stable-isotope assignment, after which we will work through an example R script where we will, step-by-step, work though the procedures to determine the likely origins of unknown-origin migrants. No data is required by participants as everything will be provided during the workshop, but participants are welcome to apply the code to their own data.
The expected outcome for this workshop is that participants will gain a better understanding for the general approach and theory behind stable-isotope assignment using hydrogen isotopes and leave with some fundamental R code to build upon for their own analyses.


Target audience
Researchers and students who are interested in or are planning to collect tissues for stable isotope assignment. This workshop is aimed at a general audience.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some familiarity with R/Rmarkdown is suggested.
