title: Meeting Code of Conduct
text:
This Code of Conduct is intended to set clear expectations of behavior at the 2026 meeting of the SCO-SOC to ensure that all participants feel safe and welcome and that SCO-SOC 2026 is a positive experience for all.
The SCO-SOC welcomes everyone and celebrates diversity in all its forms. The SCO-SOC is dedicated to providing a collaborative, supportive, and engaging environment for everyone involved and that is free of discrimination, harassment, and retaliation. We expect all participants to help foster a respectful and considerate environment that provides constructive critique, debate, and interactions that respectfully allow for differences of opinion while embracing engaging discussion.

Meeting Scope
We intend for SCO-SOC 2026 to foster open, honest and engaging communication of ornithological science. In so doing, we aim to promote equal opportunity and treatment for all participants. To achieve effective communication, we require attendees to conduct themselves in a courteous fashion and respect the intellectual property of our colleagues. We represent the field of ornithology, and it is imperative that we behave as professionals toward all conference participants, including, but not limited to, conference delegates, Council members, conference volunteers, sponsors, and exhibitors.
All forms of communication among conference participants during the meeting are considered within the scope of SCO-SOC 2026 and therefore fall under the Code of Conduct. These include public and private communications, social media posts, direct messages, phone calls, and other forms of written, verbal, and non-verbal (including visual) communication. Additionally, communication as described above occurring before or after the SCO-SOC 2026 meeting but pertaining to content associated with the meeting and/or relies on contact information of a meeting participant was procured before or during the meeting may also fall under the purview of this Code of Conduct.


Expectations of Participants
Harassment in any form between participants of SCO-SOC 2026 will not be tolerated. Harassment includes any communication with, or behavior towards another participant involving offensive gestures, verbal and written comments, posts on the internet and social media, deliberate intimidation, stalking, harassing photography or recording, sustained disruption of talks or other events, inappropriate physical or electronic contact, microaggressions, and unwelcome attention. Note that it is also possible to unintentionally engage in harassment and participants must be mindful of their behavior. Participants asked to stop any harassing behavior by anyone are expected to comply immediately, regardless of their intent.


Use of Media Associated With the Meeting
By registering for and attending this Meeting, Participants agree to allow SCO-SOC 2026 to use photos, videos, or audio recordings taken of them during the Meeting in publications, promotions, and on the websites and social media pages of the participating societies. Only the Society may (a) take/make or distribute audio or video recordings of the Meeting or Participants or (b) distribute them (via social media or other means).
Participants wishing to share information from the Event and/or post photos via social media, whether of their own material or that of others, must adhere to individual social media platforms’ stated rules and policies. We ask that presenters and hosts of Events that do not want content or information shared via social media clearly communicate this to members of the audience and that members of the audience adhere to such requests.


Reporting an Incident
Any individual covered by the Code of Conduct who believes that they have been subjected to harassment, notices that someone else is being harassed, or has any other concerns about an individual’s behavior should report the incident immediately. Similarly, any breaches of the Code associated with media use should also be reported immediately. Potential violations of the Meeting Code of Conduct should be reported promptly to the SCO-SOC 2026 Safe Meeting Committee via email at president@sco-soc.ca. The Committee will strive to acknowledge all reports within one hour of receipt (between 9am to 5pm). All complaints will be taken seriously, promptly reviewed, and may be subject to investigation. Reports should be submitted using the group email, which will be directed to the entire Committee. All information related to the complaint and any subsequent investigation will be treated with the utmost confidentiality and shared only with Committee members as necessary to ensure a thorough and fair review.


Disciplinary Action
Individuals found to have engaged in behavior prohibited by this policy, as well as those making bad faith allegations under the Code of Conduct will be subject to disciplinary action. The SCO-SOC 2026 Safe Meeting Committee may take any action they deem appropriate, ranging from a verbal warning or ejection/prohibition from the specific activity in question (e.g., workshop, symposium, or even the entire conference), banning them from future conferences run or jointly run by the partner societies, revoking membership in from the Society, and/or the reporting of their behavior to their employer and research funders.


Retaliation Is Prohibited
Any form of retaliation—including seeking to violate the confidentiality of a reporting individual—against individuals who file a complaint or assist in an investigation or against any individuals suspected of doing so will not be tolerated by the SCO-SOC 2026 meeting. Retaliation is a serious violation of this policy and like any breach of the Code itself, will be subject to disciplinary action.


Questions & Appeal
Any questions regarding this policy should be directed to the SCO-SOC 2026 Safe Meeting Committee. If an individual involved in any reported incident is dissatisfied with the disciplinary action, they may appeal to a committee made of the collective members of the executive committee from the Society.


Social Media Policy
The 2026 meeting of the SCO-SOC supports the use of social media; we encourage thoughtful and considerate sharing of conference content. In our view, sharing ornithological science with the public via social media is one tool for public education and outreach and a key part of gaining long-term support for science and conservation.
We encourage presenters to include personal and/or project social media handles, project hashtags or QR codes to external content on their slides (at least the opening/title slide, but recommended to use on all slides) and posters. For those without personal/project handles or hashtags, consider including the conference hashtag (#SCOSOC2026) or a social media icon on slides to let people know you are supportive of them posting about your work on social media.
Any presenters not wanting their presentation or research to be featured in social media posts must explicitly opt out of social media: this is best achieved by placing a “no social media” symbol on slides or materials. If presenters do not opt out in this manner, it shall be implied that conference organizers and/or attendees can share published research presented at the conference without consent.
Anyone may participate in conversations on the host societies’ social media channels; however, please be aware that:

Credit must be given to presenters/researchers whose presentation and/or research are featured in your post.
The host society has the right to delete posts or comments containing spam, irrelevant remarks, or items that do not align with their mission/integrity.
Personal attacks, promotion of violence or illegal activities, offensive material, or profanity will be deleted.

The host society reserves the right to ban users who violate this policy.
Conference attendees are expected to abide by the meeting code of conduct (above), and all those engaging on social media are asked to maintain apply the same respectful, courteous, inclusive, and supportive conduct online as in person to ensure a safe, hospitable, and productive conference. Discrimination, harassment, and/or retaliation will not be tolerated.
Additionally, we recommended that presenters and those sharing on social media be mindful of how photos of birds (and other animals) and their nests may appear to the public: Are safe and taxonomically appropriate grips being used? Does the bird appear in any way to be stressed, disheveled, or in an unnatural position? For suggestions on sharing photos of birds in the hand, see guidelines provided by the North American Banding Council. In addition, ask yourself if the use of a nest photo is helping to demonstrate something regarding your methods or results rather than just providing an interesting backdrop. For further guidelines on ethical photography of birds and their nests, see Audubon’s Guide to Ethical Bird Photography and Videography.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
Despite the federal prohibition on killing migratory birds and destroying their nests, approximately 269 million birds are killed and almost one million nests are destroyed annually in Canada due to otherwise lawful human activities. Bird mortality results from window collisions, fisheries bycatch, powerline electrocution, among other causes. Nest destruction is primarily associated with vegetation management activities during the breeding season including both temporary activities such as agriculture or forestry and permanent land conversion such as urbanization. This unintentional (incidental) take includes almost all spheres of human activities, both industrial and non-industrial, and is expected to increase as human development accelerates.
In the last few years, there has been renewed interest in regulating incidental take at the federal level. A regulatory system could provide benefits to migratory birds through the universal adoption of beneficial management practices in exchange for more legal certainty. However, such an initiative requires a strong scientific foundation to ensure that decision-making achieves conservation goals. For example, understanding the scope and impact of an activity is essential for establishing a baseline against which mitigation measures can be evaluated. Further research is also needed to evaluate evidence-based mitigation measures and their applicability in the Canadian context.
This workshop will examine the concept of incidental take and will aim to foster discussion on how scientists can influence regulatory and policy development through their research. The workshop will include a presentation followed by an open discussion with participants. The expected outcome is that participants will gain a better understanding of how to present the results of their research to policymakers to better support policy development for migratory birds in Canada. The workshop may also help researchers incorporate incidental take considerations into their work and strengthen collaboration between scientists and policymakers.


Target audience
The target audience consists of researchers with an interest in policy-making and with knowledge on the effects of human activities on migratory birds.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Some prior knowledge of the prohibitions of the Migratory Birds Convention Act and the Migratory Birds Regulations 2022 is useful.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
Combine BirdNET Analyzer and Kaleidoscope Pro for robust acoustic analysis, quality assurance (QA), and custom recogniser development. We will work through two real-world workflows: (i) running automated detections for birds in BirdNET, and then using Kaleidoscope Pro for efficient manual QA, and (ii) applying Kaleidoscope’s clustering tools to generate high-quality training clips for building a custom amphibian BirdNET recognizer. Attendees will gain a clear introduction to how these two powerful software tools can be used together to leverage the strengths of each, creating an efficient and scalable workflow for acoustic monitoring. Designed for ecologists, bioacousticians, and practitioners, this Wildlife Acoustics workshop emphasizes practical skills, reproducible workflows, and confidence in automated acoustic monitoring results.


Target audience
Ecologists, bioacousticians, and practitioners.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
General knowledge of Kaleidoscope and BirdNET are helpful for this workshop.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Description
WildTrax is a free online platform developed to remove the barrier of entry for researchers and managers to manage and process ARU recordings at any scale of research program. Developed to help users manage and process acoustic data from raw recordings through to being used in statistical analyses, WildTrax allows users to store raw data, metadata, and derived species data on a cloud system that can be shared by collaborators anywhere in the world. With standardized metadata formats, processing methods and report outputs, the data can be easily stored and shared between users.
In this workshop we’ll teach you how to upload and manage acoustic recordings; store and manage metadata such as survey locations, field site visits, and field equipment information; process the recordings to identify the species vocalizing in the recordings; create and manage projects to aggregate your data into collective reports; use the built in birdsong recognizers (BirdNET and HawkEars) to enhance your processing abilities; and publish, share and download the data contained on WildTrax.
The workshop is set-up to be interactive so that users can follow along on the WildTrax platform to perform the various steps being presented using their own data or example data provided by the facilitators to learn the various features and functions available in WildTrax.


Target audience
This workshop is meant to appeal to novice passive acoustic monitoring users (basic understanding of an ARU and spectrogram) to a more experienced researcher wanting to learn how WildTrax can help with their data storage and processing needs.


Prerequisite skills/knowledge
Basic understanding of passive acoustic recordings and spectrograms is helpful.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Canadian Wildlife Service’s national wildlife management and assessment teams conduct research supporting the population monitoring and management of Canada’s migratory birds. Research centers around three overall themes: 1) optimizing applied population monitoring, for both professional and citizen science programs, as well as automated monitoring technologies; 2) developing integrated statistical methods to improve estimates of population sizes, status, trends and distribution; and 3) coordinating research and reporting with international partners to inform conservation across the full annual cycle. Ongoing and upcoming research projects involve: developing integrated spatiotemporal models of population status and drivers of trends using monitoring, remote sensing, and demographic data; developing object detection models to automate counts from seabird colony photo surveys; improving statistical models for estimating density and population sizes; improving breeding waterfowl population estimates by optimizing survey designs and accounting for bias in sex ratios; and improving surveys and models to estimate harvest of migratory birds.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
We are an ecotoxicology lab with a strong conservation focus. Our lab studies the effects of environmental contaminants and other non-pollution stressors to better understand how individual birds, populations and communities respond to threats. We use a variety of methods from captive and field controlled dosing studies, beaker and limnocorral studies on aquatic insects that are important prey, and small and big scale field experiments to assess short and long term responses to communities across the Prairie region. A major focus is on how pesticides and other agricultural stressors impact common grassland and wetland associated songbirds through altered prey, neurotoxicity, and disturbance. We also conduct research on the effects of industrial pollution to shorebirds.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Parks Canada Agency monitors birds in protected areas across Canada within a common framework called the Ecological Integrity Monitoring Program (EIMP). This program assesses the status and trend of ecological integrity of 119 ecosystems within 43 national parks across the country and can enable prioritization and evaluation of management actions to enhance ecosystem integrity. Birds are one of the most common indicators, being monitored within six different ecosystem types in 39 parks. Of the avian indicators assessed in 2025, the proportion in good, fair and poor condition was 56%, 31%, and 11%, and the proportion improving, stable and declining was 11%, 43% and 19%. We provide a brief overview of the EIMP and a summary of bird indicators within the program. We also present a case study from a protected area to demonstrate how a monitoring indicator can be developed and used in the ecosystem management planning process.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
The Avian Behaviour and Conservation Lab at the University of Manitoba investigates how birds respond behaviourally to anthropogenic environmental change. Our research explores how birds time their daily and seasonal activities, and how flexibly these schedules respond to new conditions associated with climate change. We also investigate how artificial light at night alters the timing and movement behaviour of birds. Through field-based experiments, from the Neotropics to the sub-Arctic, we study primarily migratory species, including aerial insectivores such as Purple Martin and Eastern Whip-poor-will. We also collaborate with northern Indigenous communities in Manitoba to address shared concerns regarding change in avian behaviour and populations.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
At the Wildlife Research and Monitoring Section of the Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, we coordinate three strands of avian research: the breeding ecology of shorebirds and waterfowl in the Hudson Bay Lowlands, the nutrient dynamics behind grassland bird habitat use, and climate effects on Wild Turkey distribution. Glen Brown’s work in Ontario’s Far North - one of the largest contiguous wetland systems in the world - has shown how the region may be vulnerable to the deepening of the permafrost active layer and wetland drying. Richard Feldman’s work in the Carden Alvar ecosystem has shown the connections between plant stoichiometry and variation in the quantity and quality of the prey of Eastern Whip-poor-will. Jeff Bowman’s work has focused on strategies that Ontario’s reintroduced Wild Turkeys have used to succeed in a northern climate. Combined, we contribute to conserving birds across the province, and involving students in applied ecological research.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Partners In Flight (PIF) is a network of organizations dedicated to landbird conservation. Partners range from not-for-profit organizations to academics, governments, funders, and industry. Each partner brings their strengths, capacities, and expertise to achieve conservation for our shared birds. This presentation will highlight PIF’s science-based, open access data tools such as the Avian Conservation and Assessment Database, a species conservation status assessment tool that evaluates vulnerability factors at continental and regional scales. Other initiatives include revised model for population estimates, tools to evaluate progress in achieving continental population trend objectives and maps to explore migratory connections in the absence of tracking data. Finally, we’ll focus on how these tools support adaptive management and measurable outcomes for birds and how we (including you), as the bird research and conservation community can leverage and amplify these tools and approaches for bird conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Banding and recapture of birds in the early 1900s provided the first documentation of individual bird movements in North America. In recent decades, bird monitoring has been revolutionized by technological advances such as satellite telemetry, geolocators, and automated radio telemetry (e.g., Motus), as well as the growth of ‘big data’ through participatory science, and the use of artificial intelligence for species identification. This has prompted questions about whether traditional methods such as banding have become irrelevant. On the contrary, standardized banding efforts remain fundamental to understanding longevity, annual survival rates, age structure, and physiological responses to environmental change. Banding data also support a wide range of conservation and management outcomes, including disease surveillance and assessment of habitat restoration. Since 1998, the Canadian Migration Monitoring Network has facilitated communication and collaboration among bird observatories across the country. Maintaining strong banding programs while integrating emerging technologies is critical to advancing ornithological research and conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Our research group, based at McGill University’s Macdonald Campus, investigates the link between avian movement, contaminants, physiology, and life history across many scales. Our study regions range from the Neotropics (Belize) to the Arctic (Hudson Bay), and many places in-between (Gulf of Alaska, St Lawrence system, Island of Montreal). In long-term collaboration with the McGill Bird Observatory, we investigate urban habitat use of migratory and resident songbirds around Montreal. We are also part of two long-term seabird monitoring programs at Middleton and Coats islands, where we work to understand the impacts of anthropogenic pressures on northern marine ecosystems. To answer our research questions, we combine biologging techniques (GPS, geolocators, accelerometry) and emerging technologies (drones, uncrewed surface vehicles), along with physiological biomarkers, contaminants, and doubly-labelled water experiments. Overall, our research informs management decisions and deepens our collective understanding of the natural world.

title: Presentations
text:
Presenter(s): Amy Sutley1, Alana Westwood2
Affiliation(s): 1. Dalhousie University, 2. Dalhousie University
Session: Session 2: Conservation Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:10 UTC


The population of LeConte’s sparrow (Ammospiza leconteii) is declining across the portion of its breeding range which falls in Western Canada. LeConte’s sparrow has been identified as a priority for conservation assessment and management by Canadian government agencies, but the species is poorly understood in terms of its ecology and distribution. We developed a high-resolution species distribution model (SDM) of LeConte’s sparrow occurrence in the Prairie Ecozone of Canada to investigate the habitat associations and spatial distribution of LeConte’s sparrow and identify candidate areas for land conservation. A maximum entropy (MaxEnt) method was used to predict the probability of occurrence for LeConte’s sparrow. In the presence observations dataset, 2,595 of 8,253 (31%) occurrences may have represented positional uncertainty as they were located on roads and in open bodies of water. As most SDMs rarely correct for fine-scale positional uncertainty, we tested three different correction distances (relocating observations to adjacent habitat). We compared three different models (no relocations; relocations within 30m; relocations within 100m) and found that they performed similarly. Covariates used to predict occurrence included proximity to wetlands, land use, elevation, mean summer precipitation, and a normalized difference vegetation index. Model performance and output was similar across corrections, and we selected the 100m correction to maximize sample size. Probability of occurrence for LeConte’s sparrow showed a strong association with low elevation prairie wetlands and riparian areas, including urban rivers. To develop recommendations for land conservation, we identified seven priority locations where existing protected areas could be expanded to include potential habitat for LeConte’s sparrow. We encourage managers to field-validate and apply our model to inform habitat protection for this species.

title: Presentations
section: An investigation into how Golden-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia atricapilla) movement and survival in overwintering habitats differs along an urbanization gradient
text:
An investigation into how Golden-crowned Sparrow (Zonotrichia atricapilla) movement and survival in overwintering habitats differs along an urbanization gradient
Presenter(s): Dilan Praat1, Dr David Green2, Dr Elizabeth Gow3
Affiliation(s): 1. Simon Fraser University, 2. Simon Fraser University, 3. Environment and Climate Change Canada
Session: 3MT - Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 20:44 UTC

Abstract
Urban habitats offer many unique opportunities and challenges to various bird species. With the global land-cover of cities expected to double over the next 25 years, it is crucial to understand how birds are surviving and moving in urban landscapes. Past research on urban settings has focused on the survival and reproductive success of breeding birds. There is significantly less research into the movement and survival of songbirds overwintering in urban areas. This discrepancy is important as many species spend large portions of their life-cycle in there wintering ranges, and this may also be the time when food and predation pressures are at there highest. We studied how Golden-crowned sparrow Zonotrichia atricapilla movement and survival differs from rural parks to urban neighborhoods in Metro-Vancouver. 30 birds were radio-tagged across five sites in the winter of 2025-2026, and an additional 200+ birds were colour-banded across six sites from 2021-2026. We tracked the radio-tagged birds for six weeks to obtain details on fine-scale movements to determine habitat use and home range size, and to ascertain known-fate survival. Reported colour-band resightings were used to estimate broad overwintering Golden-crowned sparrow apparent-survival. We found that areas of increased urbanization had lower rates of known-fate survival and higher rates of unexplained disappearances. Birds initially caught in the proximity of static bird feeders had smaller home ranges than the home ranges of birds that were not caught in close proximity to feeders. Through colour-band resightings, we found that birds overwintering in areas with higher rates of urbanization had lower rates of apparent-survival than those living in rural areas. These findings indicate that while urban habitats are suitable for overwintering Golden-crowned sparrows, these benefits are mitigated by potential survival risks, and more research is needed to understand the mechanics of these relationships.

title: Presentations
section: Assessing Population Trends and Structure of a Cryptic Waterbird Across its Range
text:
Assessing Population Trends and Structure of a Cryptic Waterbird Across its Range
Presenter(s): Joe Brosseau1, Joseph Brosseau2
Affiliation(s): 1. Biology MSc Student, University of Saskatchewan, 2. Department of Biology, University of Saskatchewan
Session: 3MT - Ecology: Populations
Time: 2026-10-06 20:24 UTC

Abstract
The Forster’s Tern (Sterna forsteri) is an understudied North American waterbird with an indeterminate population status in potential decline. Compared to other North American Tern species, Forster’s Terns have shorter migrations, staying within North America throughout the annual cycle. The core of the Forster’s Tern breeding range is in interior wetlands of the Prairie Pothole Region, with additional breeding populations ranging across the southern Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico coasts of the United States. My research aims to improve our knowledge of Forster’s Tern population structure and movement across the full annual cycle, including determining whether different subspecies exist, as was proposed more than 80 years ago. For this, I have two objectives: 1) assess population trends in relation to environmental covariates with the use of Citizen Science and remotely sensed environmental data, and 2) analyze population structure with the use of a combination of morphological and genetic data collected across their breeding populations. These analyses together will allow for a more complete understanding of Forster’s Terns, providing insight into their population status and structure across the annual cycle and helping determine whether separate populations should be treated as separate “Designatable Units” for the most optimal conservation and management strategies for the species.

title: Presentations
section: Assessing toxic metal contamination and trophic-level transfer in the Deka and Lukosi rivers using fish and predatory birds as bioindicators
text:
Assessing toxic metal contamination and trophic-level transfer in the Deka and Lukosi rivers using fish and predatory birds as bioindicators
Presenter(s): Mavis Gavajena1, 2
Affiliation(s): 1. MSc candidate, Faculty of Agriculture, Environment and Natural Resources Management, Midlands State University
Session: 3MT - Pollution / Ecotoxicology
Time: 2026-10-06 20:36 UTC

Abstract
Freshwater ecosystems are increasingly threatened by contamination from toxic elements such as arsenic, manganese and lead, largely driven by mining, industrial discharge and agricultural activities. These pollutants can persist in aquatic environments, accumulating in sediments and entering food webs, where they pose risks to aquatic organisms and higher trophic levels. In river systems such as the Deka and Lukosi, which are influenced by anthropogenic activities, there is growing concern about the extent of contamination and its ecological implications.
Aquatic organisms, particularly fish, play a critical role in transferring contaminants through trophic interactions, while predatory aquatic birds may serve as effective bioindicators of environmental pollution due to their position at the top of the foodweb. Despite this, limited information exists on the distribution and bioaccumulation of toxic elements within these river systems and their potential magnification across trophic levels.
This study aims to investigate the concentrations of arsenic, manganese and lead in water, sediment and fish within the Deka and Lukosi rivers, and to assess their subsequent bioaccumulation in predatory aquatic birds. We hypothesize that contaminant levels will vary spatially and that bioaccumulation will increase with trophic position, reflecting biomagnification processes.
By linking environmental contamination to biological uptake across multiple trophic levels, this research seeks to provide insight into ecosystem health and the potential risks posed to aquatic biodiversity and avian species, while informing future monitoring and conservation strategies.

title: Presentations
section: Balancing act: ATP supply and demand in torpid ruby-throated hummingbirds
text:
Balancing act: ATP supply and demand in torpid ruby-throated hummingbirds
Presenter(s): Amalie Hutchinson1, James Staples2, Chris G Guglielmo3
Affiliation(s): 1. Western University, 2. Western University, 3. Western University
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 15:50 UTC

Abstract
ATP supply by mitochondria and ATP demand by cellular processes is carefully regulated during active periods and during states of metabolic suppression, such as torpor. Torpor is a state of inactivity characterized by decreased metabolic rate (MR) and body temperature that can be spontaneously reversed using endogenously produced heat. To avoid the high cost of thermoregulation at night, hummingbirds use torpor. We searched for a site of metabolic suppression in the flight muscle of torpid ruby-throated hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris). We were the first to investigate mitochondrial dynamics in hummingbirds. OXPHOS was suppressed by ~20% through CI when pyruvate was the metabolic fuel, but no suppression was observed when mitochondria were fueled with a lipid-based substrate. As fat is the main source of energy during torpor, we concluded that, unlike mammalian models of torpor, whole-animal MR suppression does not involve downregulating mitochondria. Next, we investigated ATP demand pathways to determine if inhibiting SERCA or Na+/K+ ATPase drives torpor. SERCA activity did not change, however, the uncoupler sarcolipin was more highly phosphorylated. Phosphorylation inhibits sarcolipin, resulting in decreased ATP demand and heat generation. Na+/K+ ATPase activity decreased by 43% in torpor, a mechanism that could account for a significant proportion of whole-animal MR suppression. Taken together, we suggest that torpid hummingbirds suppress pathways of ATP demand in concert with passive metabolic suppression initiated by adjusting thermoregulation and allowing core body temperature to drop. These findings highlight interesting contrasts between birds and mammals and provide insight into their evolutionary paths to heterothermy.

title: Presentations
section: Beyond habitat amount: Narrow seismic lines fragment habitat for a declining old-forest songbird
text:
Beyond habitat amount: Narrow seismic lines fragment habitat for a declining old-forest songbird
Presenter(s): Taylor Hart1, Juan Andrés Martinez Lanfranco2, Alessandro Franceschini3, Erin Bayne4
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Alberta, 2. University of Alberta, 3. University of Alberta, 4. University of Alberta
Session: Session 2: Habitat Use and Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 19:10 UTC

Abstract
Habitat loss and fragmentation are primary drivers of forest degradation and biodiversity decline, but disentangling their effects is challenging because they co-occur, may interact, and are perceived differently by different species, requiring species-specific definitions and explicit tests for additive and interactive effects. To quantify the effects of these processes on Black-throated Green Warblers (BTNW), a species of conservation concern in Alberta, we developed species-specific definitions of BTNW habitat (80–140 year old mixedwood forest) and fragmentation (edge density). We compared spatial occupancy models with habitat amount only, edge density only, and their additive and interactive effects using three increasingly comprehensive definitions of fragmentation (large polygonal disturbances only; adding wide linear features >8 m; and all anthropogenic disturbances including narrow 2–8 m seismic lines), at three spatial scales (7, 78, and 314 ha). The most comprehensive definition, including seismic lines, provided the best model fit at the 7 and 78 ha scales, indicating BTNW perceive even narrow disturbances as habitat boundaries. Edge density negatively affected occupancy at the two finer scales, but habitat amount became the dominant predictor at the broader 314 ha scale. Our species-specific approach revealed responses that generic classifications would likely obscure, demonstrating that conservation strategies for this species must consider spatial configuration alongside habitat amount. Given the strong negative effects of edge density and major population declines reported for BTNW in Alberta, we urge managers to minimize cumulative edge creation through harvest planning and active seismic line regeneration.

title: Presentations
section: Beyond occupancy: evaluating whether forestry best management practices support successful reproduction of Endangered Williamson’s Sapsucker
text:
Beyond occupancy: evaluating whether forestry best management practices support successful reproduction of Endangered Williamson’s Sapsucker
Presenter(s): Tory Hartley-Cox1, Elizabeth Gow2, Emily Choy3
Affiliation(s): 1. PhD Student, McMaster University, 2. Environment and Climate Change Canada, 3. McMaster University
Session: 3MT - Species at Risk
Time: 2026-10-06 20:40 UTC

Abstract
Forest management practices designed to reduce the impacts of logging on wildlife may not always provide the habitat conditions necessary for successful reproduction. In some cases, retained habitat may continue to attract breeding individuals while failing to support reproductive success, potentially creating ecological traps. For the federally Endangered Williamson’s Sapsucker (Sphyrapicus thyroideus), forestry best management practices (BMPs) have been developed for use in British Columbia. However, these voluntary practices are applied only within the species’ known area of occupancy, and their effectiveness in supporting successful reproduction has never been evaluated. To determine whether current forestry BMPs provide habitat that supports successful reproduction, we are linking nest productivity to habitat characteristics, focusing on nesting and foraging conditions in both managed and unmanaged forests. During the 2025 and 2026 breeding seasons, occupancy surveys were conducted throughout the Princeton and Boundary regions of southern British Columbia to locate breeding territories and active nest cavities. Nest productivity was monitored using repeated visual observations, custom-built cavity cameras, and acoustic recording units to document clutch size, hatching success, fledging success, and nest failure. Habitat assessments quantified nest-tree characteristics, stand structure, and surrounding forest composition across protected forests, retention-harvested stands, and unlogged forests. This project will provide the first direct evaluation of whether current forestry BMPs support the successful reproduction of Williamson’s Sapsucker in Canada. By identifying the nesting and foraging habitat characteristics associated with nest success and failure, the results will help guide future refinements to forestry BMPs and inform recovery planning and long-term conservation of this Endangered species.

title: Presentations
section: Can supplemental feeders be used to study caching behavior? A field study in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus)
text:
Can supplemental feeders be used to study caching behavior? A field study in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus)
Presenter(s): Ipshita Gayen1, Kimberley Mathot2
Affiliation(s): 1. PhD Student, University of Alberta, 2. University of Alberta; Canada Research Chair, Integrative Ecology
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 15:40 UTC

Abstract
Small parids like black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) rely on caching (i.e. storing food for later use) as a strategy to mitigate starvation risk during winter. Although caching can occur throughout the autumn and winter, it is predicted that most intense period should occur in late summer/early fall, when natural food availability is high, daylength is long, and ambient temperatures are favourable to both meet immediate energetic needs and invest in building up caches. Quantifying caching in free-living birds is time consuming, and thus, relatively few studies have quantified seasonal peaks in caching. Here, we assess if feeders can be used to capture seasonal peaks in caching investment using automated detections of black-capped chickadees fitted with passive integrated transponders to quantify caching in late summer -early fall. From previous studies and theoretical calculations, the number of sunflower seeds required to meet daily energetic requirements at this time of year is estimated to be ~45 seeds, and thus, daily feeder visits in excess of 45 can be inferred to indicate caching. We tested theoretical predictions about seasonal caching peaks, the effect of temperature and differences between sexes. We found that both day in season and temperature play important roles in shaping seasonal caching patterns as predicted, but contrary to theoretical predictions, females invested less in caching than males. Further, the observed seasonal peak in caching using feeders was much shorter compared caching peaks in populations without supplemental food. Our findings demonstrate that feeder-based studies can capture biologically meaningful variation in caching behaviour, with some important caveats, and highlight the combined influence of seasonal and short-term energetic factors on food-caching strategies.

section: Classification of egg laying, incubation and brood rearing from remotely collected telemetry data
text:
Classification of egg laying, incubation and brood rearing from remotely collected telemetry data
Presenter(s): Ilsa Griebel1, Érika G da Rocha2, Abigail Butler3, Laura R Dykstra4, Cassidy L Waldrep5, John M Coluccy; Patrick K Devers6, Min T Huang7, Tracy A G Rittenhouse8, Joshua C Stiller9, Jacob N Straub10, Mitch D Weegman11
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Saskatchewan, 2. University of Saskatchewan, 3. SUNY Brockport, 4. University of Connecticut, 5. University of Saskatchewan, 6. Ducks Unlimited, Inc, 7. USFS, 8. Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, 9. University of Connecticut, 10. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, 11. SUNY Brockport, 12. University of Saskatchewan
Session: Session 1: Methods Matter
Time: 2026-10-06 16:50 UTC

Abstract
Knowledge of reproductive attempts and outcomes is imperative for understanding drivers of population growth and learning how individual decisions and environmental conditions explain variation in productivity, but breeding locations in remote areas of the planet can hinder our ability to monitor reproductive attempts using traditional methods. The goal of this study was to develop a data-driven, machine-learning method that identified egg laying, incubation and brood rearing behaviour for two species of dabbling duck, American black ducks (Anas rubripes) and mallards (A. platyrhynchos), to measure reproductive success remotely using Global Positioning System (GPS) and tri-axial acceleration (ACC) data collected by tracking devices. We successfully developed an egg laying/early incubation model (classified as nesting or not), a full-term incubation model (non-incubating, failed incubation attempt or successful incubation attempt) and early (1-15 days post-hatch) and late (16-30 days post-hatch) brood rearing models (combined output as failed or fledged brood), which all had overall accuracies >94%. We applied our method to two large-scale datasets collected in eastern North America on black ducks and mallards and summarized data by species, age and year. We found mallards had greater breeding success than black ducks, due to higher nest propensity and brood fledging success. For each species, after second year females had higher nest propensity, nest success, and brood fledging success than second year females. Our method can be used to understand multiple fine-scale metrics of reproductive success using retrospective analysis of tracking data, should be applicable to most dabbling duck species, and could be adjusted for other taxa equipped with tracking devices that display restricted movements during breeding. Results from this approach allow hypothesis tests of environmental drivers of productivity and evaluations of their contributions to population change.

section: Colour Preferences in the Selection of Anthropogenic Nesting Materials in European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris)
text:
Colour Preferences in the Selection of Anthropogenic Nesting Materials in European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris)
Presenter(s): KC Collings1, Colleen Barber2, Gabrielle Armstrong3, Katelyn Eisner4, Olivia Smith5, Freya Binney6
Affiliation(s): 1. Saint Mary’s University, 2. Saint Mary’s University, 3. Saint Mary’s University, 4. Saint Mary’s University, 5. Saint Mary’s University, 6. Saint Mary’s University
Session: Session 1: Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 15:30 UTC

Abstract
Urban birds often incorporate anthropogenic materials into their nests. However, the factors that determine material selection remain unclear. Visual cues, such as colour, may influence birds’ choice of nesting material. European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris), are a cavity-nesting songbird species observed to incorporate anthropogenic materials into their nests. Males build most of the nest as means to attract a mate and females help finish the construction. Although materials can be selected and added to nests, they can also later be thrown out rather than being further incorporated. This study investigates whether wild starlings exhibit a preference for certain colours of anthropogenic nesting materials. We provided birds with equal opportunity to select ribbons of five different colours (blue, gold, black, silver and white) and quantified both the colours selected from the environment and those incorporated into nests. Preliminary results indicate that certain colours are selected more often than others. Understanding the mechanisms underlying anthropogenic material selection in birds’ nests will improve our understanding of behavioural adaptations in urban environments and better inform conservation strategies.

title: Presentations
section: Diet of Bobolinks (Dolichonyx oryzivorus) during fall staging
text:
Diet of Bobolinks (Dolichonyx oryzivorus) during fall staging
Presenter(s): Charlotte Toner1, Wendy Monk2, Joe Nocera3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of New Brunswick, 2. University of New Brunswick, 3. University of New Brunswick
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 16:30 UTC

Abstract
Agricultural ecosystems present complex trade-offs between human and conservation priorities, especially for migratory or at-risk species whose life cycles depend on managed habitats. Many avian species can provide valuable ecosystem services in agroecosystems, such as pest and weed control, yet these roles are often poorly quantified, especially during energetically demanding periods such as prior to migration. The Bobolink (Dolichonyx oryzivorus) is a long-distance migratory grassland passerine and species-at-risk with a distinct knowledge gap surrounding its dietary function within ecosystems, as well as its dietary patterns during pre-migratory staging. My study examines Bobolink diet during the post-breeding, pre-migratory staging period of July and August. I collected fecal samples across eight agricultural sites in the Annapolis Valley of Nova Scotia, Canada. Using DNA metabarcoding of fecal samples, I identified the dietary composition of plants and insects over time, between age groups, and in relation to plant origin and insect pest status. My results indicate that the Bobolink consumes a diverse dietary community of both plants and insects, including weeds and pests. This composition shifted significantly over time as migration approached, and insect dietary composition differed significantly between adults and juveniles. This study provides the first DNA metabarcoding analysis of the Bobolink, as well as the first fine-scale identification of the fall staging diet of the Bobolink. Together, these findings indicate that the Bobolink may contribute ecosystem services within agroecosystems while simultaneously shifting its diet to meet the energetic demands of migratory staging. By contributing to the knowledge of the Bobolink during a potentially limiting period of the life cycle, I hope to improve conservation management techniques by identifying important prey sources and emphasizing the value of this species-at-risk in agricultural ecosystems.

section: Disrupted Nights, Disrupted Minds: Effects of ALAN on What, Where, and When Memory in Black-capped Chickadees
text:
Disrupted Nights, Disrupted Minds: Effects of ALAN on What, Where, and When Memory in Black-capped Chickadees
Presenter(s): Aastha Saini1, Scott A MacDougall-Shackleton2
Affiliation(s): 1. Department of Biology, University of Western Ontario; Advanced Facility for Avian Research, University of Western Ontario, 2. Department of Psychology, University of Western Ontario; Advanced Facility for Avian Research, University of Western Ontario
Session: 3MT - Behaviour / Behavioural ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 20:00 UTC

Abstract
Daily rhythms of light and dark regulate most biological processes and synchronize our internal physiology with the external environment. Artificial light at night (ALAN) has become a rapidly growing environmental pollutant, disrupting these rhythms. This disruption can adversely impact humans and wildlife, especially by disturbing the sleep-wake cycle, leading to cognitive implications that impact memory consolidation. Our research investigates the impact of ALAN on memory consolidation in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus), a passerine songbird that relies heavily on spatial memory for winter survival. Previous studies have revealed that black-capped chickadees show what, where, and when memory. For my study, I manipulated the light-dark cycles and monitored the changes in their cognition by performing WWW memory tasks. Initially, the birds searched for sunflower seeds and mealworms in trees in an indoor aviary. Then these birds were allowed to revisit those sites after either short (3 hrs) or long (125 hrs) retention intervals, and their preference for food type was recorded. We hypothesized that birds would prefer mealworms during SRI and seeds during LRI, as the mealworms in LRI were degraded, and also higher light intensity will impair their WWW memory. Preliminary data showed that control birds preferred mealworms in their first four choices for both SRI and LRI, but this was not true for the other two treatments. Further data collection is needed to confirm these trends. By demonstrating that low-intensity light pollution can degrade sleep and memory in a diurnal species, this study highlights the need to reevaluate how artificial lighting affects the cognition and behaviour of wildlife.

section: Distinguishing migratory stopover patterns across Blackpoll Warbler populations
text:
Distinguishing migratory stopover patterns across Blackpoll Warbler populations
Presenter(s): Jax Nasimok1, Maggie MacPherson2
Affiliation(s): 1. MSc Student, Trent University, 2. Trent University
Session: Session 1: Migration
Time: 2026-10-06 19:10 UTC

Abstract
Blackpoll Warblers (Setophaga striata; blackpolls) are one of the fastest declining passerines in North America. We lack clarity on which conservation issues are responsible for their documented decline of 92% in the past 50 years. The crosswise long-distance migration pattern of blackpolls is unique among neotropical migrants. From migration theory, we should expect that populations with longer migrations will face higher mortality rates. However, recent research has discovered the opposite. Eastern breeding blackpoll populations migrate the shortest distance and are declining significantly faster than western populations. Here, I extend what we know about blackpoll migration by using the Motus network to determine what habitat blackpolls are using during their southward migration. As part of long-term research on a collaborative research team, Motus tags are being deployed on blackpolls in Alaska, Manitoba, Québec, and Newfoundland. I will present an assessment of migration habitat quality that uses remote sensing data to quantify habitat characteristics surrounding Motus towers that blackpolls from each population pass by during their post-breeding migrations south. Future work will assess how apparent annual survival is correlated with different paces of migration, migration habitat quality, and wintering location from across the blackpoll range. Insights from this research will support regionally targeted conservation actions to improve outcomes for this rapidly declining songbird.

title: Presentations
section: Do black-capped chickadees behave as predicted by optimal sampling models when tracking food availability?
text:
Do black-capped chickadees behave as predicted by optimal sampling models when tracking food availability?
Presenter(s): Megan LaRocque1, Jan Wijmenga2, Kimberley Mathot3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Alberta, 2. University of Alberta, 3. University of Alberta
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 16:20 UTC

Abstract
Animals face uncertainty in every aspect of their lives. Where is the best territory? Who is the best available mate? When and where will food be available? To mitigate this uncertainty, one strategy organisms can adopt is to ‘sample’; updating their information about the state of territories, mates, and/or resources within their environment. Optimal sampling models ask: what sampling strategy should individuals adopt to maximize their fitness? In a foraging context, we can imagine an individual that encounters a patch that has recently become unprofitable. This individual must then decide how it should behave amidst this uncertainty in food availability. Should it revisit (i.e., sample) this patch later to see if the patch becomes profitable, or should it visit an alternative food patch? If an individual samples the previously encountered unprofitable patch, and the patch remains unprofitable, the individual suffers from sampling error costs. If an individual instead visits an alternative patch, but the initially unprofitable patch is now profitable, the individual misses out on exploiting this now profitable patch and experiences missed opportunity costs. Theory predicts that both sampling error and missed opportunity costs will influence individual sampling frequency. We tested these predictions using feeder visit data from a free-living winter population of black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus). We assessed how chickadee sampling frequency at empty feeders changed as a function of several variables predicted a priori to affect sampling error and/or missed opportunity costs. We found that although some factors influenced sampling frequency as predicted by optimal sampling theory, others did not. I discuss these results and propose explanations for how individual differences in sampling behaviour may influence fitness in our chickadee population.

section: Does wildfire-driven habitat fragmentation affect the population genetic structure of the Black-capped Chickadee Poecile atricapillus?
text:
Does wildfire-driven habitat fragmentation affect the population genetic structure of the Black-capped Chickadee Poecile atricapillus?
Presenter(s): Nikeet Pradhan1, Theresa M Burg2
Affiliation(s): 1. Department of Biological Sciences, University of Lethbridge, 2. Department of Biological Sciences, University of Lethbridge
Session: Session 2: Habitat Use and Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 19:20 UTC

Abstract
Wildfire is a crucial primary disturbance in many forest ecosystems; however, anthropogenic climate change has increased its intensity, extent, and severity, drastically altering wildlife habitat and connectivity. These rapid and large-scale disturbances reduce habitat availability and impede dispersal pathways in the landscape. For forest-dependent species, it results in reduced gene flow, decreasing environmental fitness and adaptation. Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus) is a resident forest species in North America, with limited dispersal and dependence on forest resources for survival, making it vulnerable to habitat fragmentation. Our study will focus on evaluating the genetic consequences of wildfire-driven habitat fragmentation in the Black-capped Chickadee by comparing genetic diversity, population connectivity, and levels of inbreeding pre- and post-fires. Our study will be conducted in central British Columbia (CBC), which has had a number of wildfire events in the last decade. We will be sampling five different sites relatively close to sites where samples were collected before the wildfire events, and genetically distinct populations were recorded. We will be using restriction-site associated DNA sequencing data to compare genetic patterns pre- and post-fires. Our study will provide a better understanding of how wildfire-induced habitat fragmentation impacts forest-dependent species population connectivity and will help inform targeted post-fire corridor restoration and conservation planning for forest-dependent species.

section: Estimating exposure to urban landscapes through a full annual cycle in two warbler species with geolocators and Motus
text:
Estimating exposure to urban landscapes through a full annual cycle in two warbler species with geolocators and Motus
Presenter(s): Nathanya Goudreau1, Kyle Elliott & Barbara Frei2
Affiliation(s): 1. McGill University, 2. McGill University, 3. Environment and Climate Change Canada
Session: 3MT - Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 20:48 UTC

Abstract
Many migratory bird populations face ongoing declines, driven by various factors including anthropogenic threats such as cat predation, collisions, and pollution. The magnitude of their exposure to some of these threats in urban landscapes across their annual cycle remains poorly understood. We aim to quantify the urban exposure throughout the annual cycle of the urban-tolerant Yellow Warblers (Setophaga petechia) and more urban-avoidant Chestnut-sided Warblers (S. pensylvanica). We predict that a species’ association with urban areas on the breeding grounds is indicative of their exposure during the rest of the annual cycle. To test if Yellow Warblers may be more exposed to urban areas throughout the year, we deployed archival light-level geolocators on breeding birds (n=88), and radio tags on migrating individuals (n=73) in Quebec, Canada. Geolocators and radio tags revealed that Chestnut-sided warblers breeding in southern Quebec migrate along the Eastern coast and winter in Costa Rica and Nicaragua, while Yellow warblers migrate further west and winter in Colombia and Venezuela. We suggest that Chestnut-sided Warblers have the highest urban exposure during migration, and have a more urbanized migratory path than Yellow Warblers, which breed and winter in more anthropogenically disturbed sites than Chestnut-sided Warblers.

section: Female black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) expand foraging both temporally and spatially to mitigate interference competition
text:
Female black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) expand foraging both temporally and spatially to mitigate interference competition
Presenter(s): Elène Haave Audet1, Kimberley Mathot2
Affiliation(s): 1. Université du Québec à Montréal, 2. University of Alberta
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 16:00 UTC

Abstract
Group living provides many potential benefits but can also incur important costs via competition for access to resources. Even in the absence of resource depletion, interference competition can reduce access to resources, and interference competition is not expected to affect all group members equally. In groups with dominance hierarchies, dominant individuals have priority access to resources and are therefore expected to experience lower costs of interference competition compared to subordinate individuals. We observed foraging behaviour in a population of 126 marked black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) at the University of Alberta Botanic Garden, near Edmonton, AB. We assessed the effect of manipulating the number of feeders available with ad libitum food on chickadee feeding territories, which we assumed would affect competition intensity, on total daily feeder visits. As predicted, we found strong evidence of interference competition: reducing feeder availability by 50% reduced average per capita daily visits to feeders in our population by circa 50%. Because chickadee flocks exhibit linear dominance hierarchies, with males being dominant over females, and at least in some populations, adults being dominant over immatures, we also investigated whether there was evidence for sex- and/or age-related differences in the strength of interference competition. We found that reductions in total daily feeder visits under lower manipulated food availability were similar for all age-sex categories, suggesting that females and immatures did not experience higher interference competition despite their subordinate status relative to males and adults. Post-hoc analyses revealed that adult females expanded their foraging area, while immature females increased both the length of their foraging window and their foraging area, when the availability of feeders was reduced. We suggest that these results may indicate that females invest more to mitigate competition and manage unpredictable access to food due to their subordinate status.

section: Fine dining: Foraging factors affecting ecosystem monitoring using seabirds
text:
Fine dining: Foraging factors affecting ecosystem monitoring using seabirds
Presenter(s): Alana Krug-MacLeod1, Jonas Hentati-Sundberg2, Kyle Elliott3
Affiliation(s): 1. McGill University University, 2. Swedish University of Agricultural Sciences, 3. McGill University University
Session: 3MT - Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 20:28 UTC

Abstract
Seabirds are central place foragers, and can be good indicators of prey distribution in regions such as the Arctic, where direct monitoring of prey is challenging. However, different species of seabirds make specific foraging decisions based on different combinations of factors. For example, in selecting forage locations, common murres have been observed to use both memory (foraging at sites with persistent prey) and local enhancement (foraging where conspecifics are feeding) more than information exchange at the colony. Since forage site characteristics versus colony characteristics are key for common murre foraging choice, our study focussed on at-sea factors potentially affecting foraging seabirds. We monitored thick-billed murres (Uria lomvia) and their prey at and around two Canadian Arctic islands that support different sized thick-billed murre colonies. We attached biologgers to murres’ lower back or tail feathers at the nesting sites and deployed a remotely-monitored, uncrewed sailing vessel (Sailbuoy) equipped with an echosounder to record prey presence along the Sailbuoy’s route. By overlaying GPS-linked accelerometry and hydroacoustic data collected over the same time period, we were able to test the match between thick-billed murres’ foraging effort and the spatial persistence of prey over the breeding season. This information will allow for real world comparison of seabird foraging routes and prey distribution, and reveal more about which factors affect how to use seabirds as indicators to assess the stability of ecosystems that are difficult to monitor directly.

title: Presentations
section: From Collection to Conservation: Expert Perspectives on the Volunteer-Contributed Bird Data Lifecycle
text:
From Collection to Conservation: Expert Perspectives on the Volunteer-Contributed Bird Data Lifecycle
Presenter(s): Elizabeth Porter1, Adam C Smith2, Shoshanah Jacobs3, Shelby Bohn4, Karl Cottenie5
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Guelph, 2. Canadian Wildlife Service, 3. University of Guelph, 4. University of Calgary, 5. University of Guelph
Session: Session 2: Conservation Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:50 UTC

Abstract
Volunteer science is foundational to long-term avian monitoring; yet, without clear understanding of volunteer characteristics, complex strategies to model observer effects remain a necessary but compromised avenue for advancing ornithological research. I address this by investigating how observer characteristics are navigated across the data lifecycle. My previous research 1) quantified influence of observer characteristics on population trend estimates, and 2) found that 51% of uses of Canadian volunteer-contributed bird data in the peer-reviewed literature do not explicitly address the volunteer nature of the data. This study examines the perspectives of experts across stages of the data lifecycle, using interviews and reflexive thematic analysis to identify practical and epistemic constraints shaping how observer characteristics are operationalized in practice. Situating these effects within real-world data management constraints informs methodological improvements and transparent reporting standards in ornithological research. This presentation will discuss potential explanations for the lack of transparency identified in the literature, the diversity of approaches used across programs to ensure reliable data from planning stages through to end-use, and what experts might do differently given unlimited resources. These findings will help bridge the gap between statistical methods for addressing observer variation and their practical application in ornithology, supporting appropriate and respectful use of volunteer-contributed bird data for evidence-based conservation.

title: Presentations
section: Heat tolerance in temperate birds: predicting their vulnerability to climate change
text:
Heat tolerance in temperate birds: predicting their vulnerability to climate change
Presenter(s): Nathan Bernier1, Anand Sachin2, François Vézina3
Affiliation(s): 1. BSc Student, Université du Québec à Rimouski, 2. Université du Québec à Rimouski, 3. Université du Québec à Rimouski
Session: 3MT - Physiology
Time: 2026-10-06 20:32 UTC

Abstract
Temperate regions are known for their short, cool spring and summer during which birds breed and must forage intensely over days to provision their offspring. Such high levels of activities increase the heat generation, which the birds must effectively dissipate to maintain their activity. However, climate warming is projected to substantially increase temperatures during the breeding period, which may cause heat stress in birds and force them to reduce their activity and thereby negatively impact nestling quality. Currently, most studies measuring the avian mechanistic responses to heat stress are from arid and desert regions, while very few studies exist on those mechanisms in birds inhabiting colder regions. As climate change increases the likelihood of extreme heat events, avian responses to higher ambient temperatures must be studied in temperate regions. In this study, we aim to measure heat dissipation capacity of pine siskins (Spinus pinus), a small resident passerine distributed across North America. During autumn 2026, we plan to measure maximum thermal conductance and heat tolerance traits i.e. evaporative heat loss, resting metabolic rate, body temperature in captive siskins while exposing them to gradually increasing temperature in a metabolic chambers. Maximum thermal conductance (Cmax), which represents the highest capacity of the bird to dissipate heat without expending additional energy, will be calculated from the body temperature, ambient temperature, oxygen consumption and water vapor loss prior to the onset of panting. Once Cmax and maximum evaporative heat dissipation capacity are quantified, we can feed them into theorical model such as the Thermoregulatory polygon. This model will allow us to predict ambient temperatures which may cause heat stress and reduce nestling provisioning, which are crucial informations to understand the effects of climate warming on temperate birds.

section: If you call them, will they come? Using playback to increase detectability of Canada Warbler in Northwestern Ontario
text:
If you call them, will they come? Using playback to increase detectability of Canada Warbler in Northwestern Ontario
Presenter(s): Vianney Cupiche1, Geovanni Balam2, Brian McLaren3
Affiliation(s): 1. Intercultural Mayan University of Quintana Roo, 2. Independent bioloogist, 3. Lakehead University
Session: Session 1: Methods Matter
Time: 2026-10-06 16:20 UTC

Abstract
Playback is commonly used to survey birds, as it is an efficient method for censusing elusive species by increasing their detection probability. However, in Ontario Breeding Atlas surveys, playback surveys are not recommended. Then, Canada Warbler Cardellina canadensis (CAWA). Within our study region, Northwestern Ontario, this species has been historically understudied and underestimated due to low accessibility, but also because these birds are small, hard to see, and spend little time during the breeding season. However, CAWA is also known as a species that is attracted by social cues; previous studies suggested CAWA uses social cues (acoustic) for habitat choices. For these reasons, my hypothesis is that the use of playback songs/calls rather than only silent point counts will increase its detection. Through our experiment, we attempted to provide a valid insight into a more effective playback method for surveying our target species. During the breeding seasons of 2021, 2022, and 2023, I implemented a bird survey protocol using a silent period followed by playback song/calls and registered the detection of the species with and without the playback. I found that in about 70% of the cases, the bird was detected mainly after playing the songs/calls. In addition, I found that the species approached but were silent in unharvested areas, whereas in post-harvest areas they used to approach singing and/or respond with territorial calls. These results suggest that using playback protocols in bird surveys will increase the likelihood of Canada Warbler detections, especially in unharvested areas, leading to more accurate population estimates.

section: Impact of ambient temperature on nestling success in a Nova Scotian population of European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) over two decades
text:
Impact of ambient temperature on nestling success in a Nova Scotian population of European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris) over two decades
Presenter(s): Janine Mombourquette1, Colleen Barber2
Affiliation(s): 1. Saint Mary’s University, 2. Saint Mary’s University
Session: Session 2: Conservation Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:30 UTC

Abstract
Birds in North America are facing steep population declines. This trend has been attributed to several anthropogenic factors, and climate change is at the forefront. Many multi-brooded species now breed earlier and have prolonged breeding seasons, extending into the hotter summer months. As a result, nestlings may face increased overheating, reductions in condition, and increased mortality. Temperature effects vary by geographic location, making localized studies necessary to understand impacts on species within a region. European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris), an urban-thriving passerine, are declining in North America. Starlings are double-brooded, with their breeding season occurring from April-July in eastern Canada. Using a wild, nest box breeding population of European Starlings in Halifax, Nova Scotia, we examined nestling condition and fledging success over two decades (2007-2026) and their relation to rising temperatures in our region. We predicted that nestling condition and fledging success would decrease over time as annual temperatures increase. We also predicted that late brood nestlings would be in poorer overall condition and have lower fledge success rates compared to those in early broods. Our long-term study will provide insight into how a bird species in Nova Scotia is responding to climate change.

title: Presentations
section: Inbreeding leads to decreased egg success hatching in cooperatively breeding Pukeko
text:
Inbreeding leads to decreased egg success hatching in cooperatively breeding Pukeko
Presenter(s): Quinlan Mann1, Mann Quinlan2, Luo Brooke3, Mugarura Abby4, Quinn James5
Affiliation(s): 1. PhD candidate, McMaster University
Session: Session 1: Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:50 UTC

Abstract
Inbreeding is the mating of two closely related individuals. Inbred offspring are more likely to receive multiple copies of the same alleles. This may lead to the expression of recessive alleles, and reductions in success. Studies of many wild bird species have shown that inbreeding can lead to decreased fitness. Pukeko are noteworthy in that they regularly engage in inbreeding in parts of their range, despite the expected fitness consequences. They are also unique in that they engage in joint-laying; a breeding system with multiple females laying eggs in a shared nest. As such, we expect that each clutch will contain some eggs that are from consanguineous pairings, and some that are not. Our study aimed to explore the consequences of inbreeding in this species. We hypothesized that we would see decreased success of inbred chicks compared to outbred ones and therefore predicted that inbred chicks would fail to hatch more often when compared to outbred ones. We performed breeding bird surveys in Tawharanui Regional Park, Auckland, New Zealand where they are known to inbreed. Once we identified breeding groups and their nests, we collected blood samples from all chicks that hatched, and tissue samples from all eggs with a developed embryo that failed to hatch. We extracted DNA from samples, then genotyped all chicks using established microsatellites for the species to calculate inbreeding coefficients. We used a generalized mixed model to determine whether inbreeding coefficient impacted the probability that a chick will hatch. We found that inbred chicks were less likely to hatch than their outbred nest mates. This shows that there are decreases in fitness that occur from the frequent inbreeding, in spite of which the Pukeko persist. This warrants future work to study other aspects of their inbreeding, and whether inbreeding impacts their fitness in other ways.

title: Presentations
section: Is it a mixedwood? Spatially-explicit responses to gradients in forest structure and composition in three boreal bird species
text:
Is it a mixedwood? Spatially-explicit responses to gradients in forest structure and composition in three boreal bird species
Presenter(s): Leonard Patterson1, Brendan Casey2, Erin Bayne3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Alberta, 2. Alberta Biodiversity Monitoring Institute, 3. University of Alberta
Session: Session 2: Habitat Use and Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 19:00 UTC

Abstract
Conventional definitions of boreal mixedwood forests are based solely on tree species composition, define species composition at a relatively coarse grain, and do not explicitly address spatial scale. Such definitions may oversimplify forest characteristics that are selected for by birds, potentially biasing past attempts to identify mixedwood habitat associations. To address this knowledge gap, we used a spatially-explicit approach to understand how three boreal bird species respond to continuous gradients in deciduous-coniferous composition, the spatial configuration of coniferous trees, and forest age within mixedwood forests in Alberta, Canada. We used a boosted regression tree model to assess the influence of these habitat characteristics across multiple spatial extents (150 m, 500 m, 1000 m) and grain sizes (5 m and 30 m) on bird relative abundance. Spatial configuration was the strongest predictor for all three species. Black-throated green warbler (Setophaga virens) and bay-breasted warbler (Setophaga castanea) responded most strongly to fine-grain, local (150 m) configuration, with abundance peaking in intimately mixed stands. Tennessee warbler (Leiothlypis peregrina) responded most strongly to configuration at the broadest extent (1000 m), also favoring intimate mixtures. The proportion of conifer and forest age consistently emerged as the second and third most important predictors, respectively. Predicted abundance on synthetic landscapes showed consistently higher abundance (~ 4-10 times higher) in intimate versus segregated mixedwoods. Our results demonstrate that species-specific and spatially-explicit mixedwood definitions that include conifer spatial configuration better capture bird habitat use than composition alone. Preserving or restoring intimate mixtures of coniferous and deciduous tree species at fine spatial scales may be particularly beneficial for our focal species.

section: Linking incubation behavior of Red-breasted Merganser (Mergus serrator) to the timing of breeding
text:
Linking incubation behavior of Red-breasted Merganser (Mergus serrator) to the timing of breeding
Presenter(s): Emilie Knighton1, Rodger Titman2, Nicolas Lecomte3, Mark Mallory and Shawn Craik4
Affiliation(s): 1. PhD Student, Université Sainte-Anne, 2. Department of Natural Resource Sciences, McGill University University, 3. Département de biologie, Université de Moncton, 4. Department of Biology, Acadia University, 5. Département des sciences, Université Sainte-Anne
Session: Session 1: Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:20 UTC

Abstract
Incubating birds are expected to balance their energetic demands with thermal requirements of developing embryos. We explored whether clutch sizes were linked to nest attendance patterns in Red-breasted Mergansers (Mergus serrator), a sea duck in which conspecific brood parasitism is common, and females are solely responsible for incubation. We used nest temperature data to determine incubation period lengths, incubation constancy, and daily frequency and duration of incubation recesses by females at 15 successful nests. Maximum clutch sizes during incubation ranged from 6 to 19 eggs and the five largest clutches were parasitized by conspecifics. Clutch size was a poor predictor of incubation parameters, but mergansers initiating incubation later in the season had 3.6 d shorter incubation periods. We hypothesize that particularly warm nest temperatures later in the season (late July-early Aug) minimized daily variation in egg temperatures, thereby leading to shorter incubation periods for late-nesting females.
