title: Presentations
section: Longer-distance migrations are not associated with higher productivity in a declining, aerial insectivore, Purple Martin (Progne subis).
text:
Longer-distance migrations are not associated with higher productivity in a declining, aerial insectivore, Purple Martin (Progne subis).
Presenter(s): Vinuri Mendis1, Joe Siegrist2, Kevin Fraser3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Manitoba, 2. Purple Martin Conservation Association, 3. University of Manitoba
Session: Session 1: Migration
Time: 2026-10-06 19:30 UTC

Abstract
Longer-distance migrations by neotropical birds are expected to be associated with higher energy costs and lower survival, but may be compensated for by more food, longer daylengths, and fewer predators at more northern latitudes, resulting in higher productivity to offset the costs. However, there have been few empirical tests of these patterns and new conditions with climate change may limit the benefits of long-distance migration. We investigated the association between migration distance and nest productivity by using a rare, 30-year dataset (1995 – 2024) of over 100,000 nest monitoring records of the eastern subspecies of purple martin (Progne subis subis), spanning their entire North American breeding range (25–54° N). We analyzed the variation in clutch size and three measures of nest success across breeding latitude (where the most northern breeders migrate the furthest). We found strong latitudinal patterns of clutch size and nest success, where the most northern and southern breeders had the highest clutch sizes and fledged the most young, with intermediate latitudes showing lower productivity. Overall, these results contrast predictions that longer-distance migrations are compensated for by higher productivity at more northern latitudes. Further, regions with lower nest success in our study align with patterns of population decline in this species, suggesting a connection between productivity and population trends in this declining aerial insectivore. These findings overall highlight the importance of considering both spatial and temporal variation when determining the effects of migration distance on reproductive success and may help to explain steeper population declines in migratory songbirds.

title: Presentations
section: Migratory stopover habitat use of songbirds in a highly urbanized green space
text:
Migratory stopover habitat use of songbirds in a highly urbanized green space
Presenter(s): Linda Nong1, Barbara Frei2, Kyle Elliott3
Affiliation(s): 1. MSc Student, McGill University University, 2. Environment and Climate Change Canada, 3. McGill University University
Session: Session 1: Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 15:40 UTC

Abstract
Urban development continues to replace natural landscapes as human populations grow, and urban landscapes are a matrix of novel resources and threats to birds. Cities are often built along migratory routes and migrating birds are further attracted to these regions by artificial light at night. Previous research has demonstrated that migrating songbirds commonly stopover in or near cities, yet there is limited information on their fine-scale habitat use during stopovers in urban green spaces. Conserving and managing these spaces is critical to provide habitat for birds during this energetically stressful period of their annual cycle. Our overall objective is to quantify stopover duration, habitat use, and diet selection of boreal-breeding passerines in a 108-ha multi-use urban park in Montreal, Canada by tagging, radio-tracking, and collecting fecal samples from birds during the post-breeding migratory period. Preliminary results from a pilot season at this park suggest that stopover lengths (9.6 ± 7.3 days, n=24) and temporary home range sizes (9.05 ± 8.75 -ha; 95% KDE, n=9) are highly variable among our eight focal species. Future analyses will include resource selection functions to quantify fine-scale habitat use and fecal DNA metabarcoding to compare diets of birds at the urban park with a nearby peri-urban site. This work is done in collaboration with local municipal land managers with the goal of providing advice on urban green space management for migratory bird conservation.

title: Presentations
section: Modernization of Bicknell’s thrush (Catharus bicknelli) survey methods using PAM with audio-classification algorithms
text:
Modernization of Bicknell’s thrush (Catharus bicknelli) survey methods using PAM with audio-classification algorithms
Presenter(s): Alexandre Ethier1, Junior Tremblay2, Marc Mazerolle3
Affiliation(s): 1. MSc student, Forest sciences, Université Laval, 2. PhD, Researcher, Environment and Climate Change Canada and affiliated professor, Université Laval, 3. Professor and researcher, Université Laval
Session: 3MT - Bioacoustics
Time: 2026-10-06 20:04 UTC

Abstract
As the need to monitor living species increases, traditional wildlife survey methods are often replaced by more efficient and less costly alternatives. Passive Acoustic Monitoring (hereafter PAM) has gained popularity in wildlife studies and is described as the gathering of acoustic data from sound-producing species virtually anywhere, at any time of day. Although this method offers crucial insights on wildlife ecology, PAM generates a large volume of data, which can be tedious since expertise and extensive effort are required to manually validate data. However, recent advances in bioacoustics allow scientists to pair PAM with audio-classification algorithms that are trained to recognize species-specific vocalizations, thereby reducing cost and resources needed. This benefits the monitoring of focal species with little-known ecology or cryptic behavior and helps expand the spatial and temporal footprint of species surveys. This is the case for the Bicknell’s thrush (Catharus bicknelli), an endangered boreal forest-dwelling bird in Canada. Most of its breeding territory is found in Québec’s highlands, at 800 m and above, in dense, regenerated balsam fir (Abies balsamea) stands. Since 2013, a mandatory survey of Bicknell’s thrush has been required to assess impact of future development projects on targeted habitat. As pressure on the species’ habitat is increasing, there is a need to adequately monitor and protect populations through more informed management mitigation measures. The main objective was to develop a standardized PAM methodology with audio-classification algorithms to efficiently process Bicknell’s thrush acoustic data on breeding grounds. The use of resulting protocol and recommendations is intended to standardize impact-assessment methods across Québec on one of the most elusive bird species in Canada. We surveyed Bicknell’s thrush in known breeding sites over four years to test and evaluate the performance of our proposed methods with different open-source algorithms.

Nest reuse by Least Flycatchers
Presenter(s): Emelie Dykstra1, Geoff Holroyd2
Affiliation(s): 1. Beaverhill Bird Observatory
Session: Session 1: Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:10 UTC

Abstract
Least Flycatchers are the most common nesting species in the aspen-balsam forest of the Beaverhill Natural Area in central Alberta. In 2022 Myrthe Van Brempt et al found that Least Flycatchers produce more eggs and young than elsewhere, have very high nest success, and have the highest breeding density in North America. Subsequently, they determined a shift to earlier autumn migration. Recently, we determined that nests were surviving the winter and being reused by Least Flycatchers. This talk will discuss the frequency and timing of nest reuse, and apparent benefits and possible risks of this unusual behavior. Nest reuse does not appear to be implicated in shift to earlier migration.

title: Presentations
section: Nest site selection of urban Spotted Towhees (Pipilo maculatus): Evidence of an ecological trap or predator shield?
text:
Nest site selection of urban Spotted Towhees (Pipilo maculatus): Evidence of an ecological trap or predator shield?
Presenter(s): Triana Hohn1, David Green2, Elizabeth Gow3
Affiliation(s): 1. Simon Fraser University, 2. Simon Fraser University, 3. Environment and Climate Change Canada
Session: Session 1: Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 15:50 UTC

Abstract
An ecological trap occurs when an animal shows a preference for a habitat that ultimately has negative fitness consequences. Birds nesting in urban areas may be particularly vulnerable to ecological traps. Alternatively, some parts of urban areas may act as shields, when human presence function as a deterrent to some common nest predators. Open-cup, ground-nesting birds are considered susceptible to disturbance from human recreation and predation by urban predators. Urban breeding Spotted Towhees (Pipilo maculatus) often nest in dense and shrubby habitat along edges, thus are a good study system to test for ecological traps. In urban areas, these edges often border walkways which may alter disturbance or predation risk due to human activity. From 2022-2025 we found and monitored 407 Spotted Towhee nests across five greenspaces of varying degree of urbanization within Metro Vancouver, British Columbia. We examined how daily nest survival and reproductive success are impacted by natural and anthropogenic factors across multiple spatial scales ranging from the level of nest sites to the entire urban greenspace. We also tested whether nesting decisions of Spotted Towhees breeding in urban greenspaces create an ecological trap or provide a shield from predation. We found that nest survival and the number of fledglings produced were both affected by weather and probability of nest survival increased with increasing degree of urbanization. We showed that Spotted Towhees preferably nest close to anthropogenic edges, like paths, but found that these edges are not functioning as a trap for towhees during the nesting stage because the distance to edge did not significantly impact nest survival or number of fledglings produced. Our findings support the hypothesis that human dominated environments benefit some native species, potentially through a shield phenomenon, highlighting the potential role urban environments can have for bird conservation.

title: Presentations
section: Nest-site selection by Hudsonian Godwits (Limosa haemastica) in the Hudson Bay Lowlands, Ontario
text:
Nest-site selection by Hudsonian Godwits (Limosa haemastica) in the Hudson Bay Lowlands, Ontario
Presenter(s): Abbey Lewis1, Glen Brown2
Affiliation(s): 1. MSc Student, Trent University, 2. Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources
Session: Session 2: Habitat Use and Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 19:40 UTC

Abstract
Climate change is expected to alter habitat suitability and increase predation risk for the federally Threatened Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) on their breeding grounds in the Hudson Bay Lowlands (HBL). Godwits have declined substantially in abundance over recent decades, but knowledge gaps regarding nesting requirements and habitat use limit conservation planning in Ontario. Our research aims to fill those gaps and investigate how variation in resource availability and predation risk on the landscape influences nest-site selection. As cryptic nesters, we expected Godwits to select for features that enhanced concealment and reduced predation risk; so, selecting for greater vegetation height, shrub cover, and distance from features like tundra ridges and trees. We collected high-resolution drone imagery covering a 70 m x 70 m area centered on fifteen Godwit nests in Polar Bear Provincial Park, Ontario from 2023 – 2025. Using that imagery, we generated land classification maps characterizing the habitat at each nest. We then tested for differences in habitat features and vegetation heights across spatial scales and between used (nest) and available sites. Findings revealed selection for nests with significantly taller vegetation within 1m2 compared to broader spatial scales and surrounding available habitat. Across all spatial scales, nests consistently featured dry graminoid fen, graminoid hummocks, and shrubs, and were rarely or never near exposed ground, flooded fen, water, trees, or ridges. Wet graminoid fen was selected against at the immediate nest site but included in the broader territory. Findings align with previous work on Alaskan and Manitoban breeding grounds, but contrastingly, no Godwits in this study nested near open water. Overall, this research provides insight into fine-scale nest-site selection by Hudsonian Godwits and suggests they may lose habitat suitability in the HBL as the boreal treeline expands northward into graminoid fen.

title: Presentations
section: Seed dispersal potential of Canadian migratory songbirds
text:
Seed dispersal potential of Canadian migratory songbirds
Presenter(s): Tamara Sturch1, Matt Fuirst and Kevin Fraser2
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Manitoba, 2. Birds Canada, 3. University of Manitoba
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 16:40 UTC

Abstract
Globally approximately 50% of woody plants rely on some form of animal mediated seed dispersal. Birds are one of the most important groups of seed dispersers due to their diversity in diet and their ability to move seeds. Movement of plants via birds has important implications for community structure and function as they can facilitate range expansions and genetic rescue for native and non-native plants. As landscape fragmentation increases and climate change advances, plant-bird interactions will have increasing significance for the adaption of plants. We are investigating the seed dispersal potential of Canadian migratory songbirds by comparing spring and fall movement of seeds, determining the potential for long distance dispersal of seeds by birds during migratory flights, and quantifying the viability of seeds dispersed by birds. We are using a combination of fecal samples collected from three migration monitoring stations in Ontario and Manitoba and stomach content analysis of window killed migratory birds collected by the Fatal Light Awareness Program in Toronto, to identify and quantify plant seeds carried by different bird species over the two migratory seasons. We assessed seed viability through tetrazolium and germination tests. Results to date indicate that 37% of fecal samples obtained from birds intercepted during migration at Long Point Bird Observatory in fall 2025, and 22% of stomach contents obtained from birds killed during fall and spring migration in Toronto 2024 contained plant seeds, including species in the genera Cornus, Juniperus, Parthenocissus, Rhamnus, Viburnum, and Vitis. Avian dispersers of plant seeds included Cedar Waxwing, Catharus thrushes, American Robin, Red-eyed Vireo, and White-throated Sparrow. These preliminary findings suggest that migratory birds may commonly move plant seeds during their migrations, shaping communities of native and non-native plants in Canada.

section: Short-term survival of mallards following external transmitter attachment
text:
Short-term survival of mallards following external transmitter attachment
Presenter(s): Cassidy Waldrep1, Madeline Ward2, John Coluccy3, Joshua Stiller4, Jacob Straub5, Nathaniel Huck6, Ted Barney7, Abigail Butler8, Austin Damminger9, Shawn Meyer10, Theodore Nichols11, Daria Sparks12, Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources13, Mathieu Tétreault14, Mitch Weegman15
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Saskatchewan, 2. University of Saskatchewan, 3. Ducks Unlimited, Inc, 4. New York State Department of Environmental Conservation, 5. SUNY Brockport, 6. Pennsylvania Game Commission, 7. Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment and Climate Change Canada, 8. SUNY Brockport, 9. New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, 10. Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment and Climate Change Canada, 11. New Jersey Fish and Wildlife, 12. SUNY Brockport, Virginia Department of Wildlife Resources, 13. Canadian Wildlife Service, Environment and Climate Change Canada, 14. University of Saskatchewan
Session: Session 1: Methods Matter
Time: 2026-10-06 16:30 UTC

Abstract
Estimating survival across different life-cycle stages is essential for contextualizing population patterns, developing species-specific conservation plans, and determining when data should be censored. This is particularly critical for migratory animals, such as waterfowl, as they experience diverse environmental conditions throughout their life. Capturing waterfowl for external transmitter attachment allows researchers to collect abundant movement and behavioural data across spatial and temporal gradients, but can expose birds to additional stress due to prolonged handling, sometimes leading to mortality. To determine if a data-censoring period is necessary and to understand the effects of the project’s capture and device attachment on mallard survival, we estimated the post-release survival of 1,263 tagged female mallards banded as part of the Eastern Mallard Project. We investigated the effects of individual bander, age, body mass, and temperature over a 15-day post-capture period using a Bayesian known-fate logistic exposure model. We found that mallards had a period survival rate of 0.97, with the greatest mortality during the first two days after capture and during extended exposure to cold temperatures, regardless of body mass or age. The majority of banders had negligible effects on daily survival, yet 12% had negative effects compared to the grand mean. We recommend that practitioners consider incorporating as few banders as feasible to deploy tracking devices for a given study design and spatial scale of deployments, because we anticipate that greater experience and consistency are easier to achieve with fewer people. Our results demonstrate the importance of contextualizing post-release survival in large tracking device projects, as environmental stressors and banding practices vary.

title: Presentations
section: Shout, shout, let it all out: Examining amplitude as a factor of negative-assortative mating in white-throated sparrows
text:
Shout, shout, let it all out: Examining amplitude as a factor of negative-assortative mating in white-throated sparrows
Presenter(s): Kyle Fisher1, Jennifer Foote2
Affiliation(s): 1. Algoma University, 2. Algoma University
Session: 3MT - Bioacoustics
Time: 2026-10-06 20:08 UTC

Abstract
Song is a crucial aspect of sexual selection in songbirds, and is often an indicator of male quality. Song amplitude is a dynamic trait that birds can vary within and among songs. However, how song amplitude variation within songs reflects song quality has not been well examined. White-throated sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis) genetic morphs (tan or white-striped) differ in their vocal behaviour but share the same two song types (up songs ascend in frequency between notes while down songs descend in frequency). Tan-striped males are preferred as mates yet sing less often than white-striped males. Thus, it is likely that differing structural components of song by morph may contribute to mate choice. Song amplitude has not been studied with respect to negative-assortative mating patterns in white-throated sparrows, nor has it been compared among up and down songs. We recorded song amplitude of white-throated sparrows using a field-portable recorder in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, in the 2025 breeding season. We measured absolute amplitude of the whole song, as well as both absolute and relative amplitude of each note using bioacoustics software. We found that morphs did not differ significantly in absolute or relative amplitude of notes. However, we demonstrate that up songs increase in amplitude across the song, while down songs decrease in amplitude across the song. White-striped males singing up songs had higher mean and minimum song amplitude than those who sang down songs. Tan-striped males did not differ in amplitude for either song type. Our preliminary work suggests that song amplitude may be a feature that receivers could use to assess morph of mates or rivals.

title: Presentations
section: Single-photon LiDAR shows promise for boreal bird habitat modelling in Ontario
text:
Single-photon LiDAR shows promise for boreal bird habitat modelling in Ontario
Presenter(s): Wren Coxson1, Jake Pott2, Baoxin Hu3, Stephen Mayor4, Jennifer Foote5
Affiliation(s): 1. Algoma University, 2. York University, 3. York University, 4. Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, Algoma University, 5. Algoma University
Session: Session 1: Methods Matter
Time: 2026-10-06 16:40 UTC

Abstract
Forest structural diversity has enabled the evolution and coexistence of diverse songbird communities in the boreal. Declines in many species have been tied to forest degradation, but we still lack a nuanced understanding of how fine scale habitat changes translate to landscape scale population impacts. Airborne laser scanning using LiDAR is quickly emerging as a tool for making this connection. Ontario has recently collected scans province-wide, using newly developed single-photon LiDAR (SPL) technology to produce a denser LiDAR dataset than is available elsewhere in Canada. Using a passive acoustic monitoring dataset from Mushkegowuk Cree territory in boreal northeast Ontario, I am completing the first multi-species test of SPL for wildlife habitat modelling. I predict that species-specific, niche-focused metrics derived from SPL data will allow more accurate species distribution modelling than has previously been possible, with some limitations imposed by lower canopy penetration of SPL than traditional LiDAR. For 91 study plots, I have calculated a set of standardized SPL habitat metrics across a range of spatial scales. By calculating single-species, single-metric response curves at each spatial scale for focal species with diverse habitat requirements, I have taken the first steps toward developing and testing niche-focused SPL metrics for boreal songbird modeling. Preliminary results show good predictive power of many test metrics for species using tree trunk and upper canopy niches, with species-specific differences in response to individual metrics that make biological sense. For shrub and forest floor associated species, few metrics have significant predictive power, but there still appear to be avenues for developing effective niche-focused metrics. This paves the way for comparisons of species distribution models using field data, basic SPL habitat metrics, and more refined niche-focused metrics.

title: Presentations
section: Smells like brood parasitism: a field experiment testing Northern Yellow Warbler responses to Brown-headed Cowbird odour at the nest
text:
Smells like brood parasitism: a field experiment testing Northern Yellow Warbler responses to Brown-headed Cowbird odour at the nest
Presenter(s): David Burghardt1, Leanne Grieves2
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Saskatchewan, 2. University of Saskatchewan
Session: Session 1: Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:30 UTC

Abstract
Brood parasitism is when an individual lays their eggs in another’s nest, imposing the costs of raising those offspring on the parasitized individual (the host). In North America, northern yellow warblers (Setophaga aestiva) are frequently parasitized by brown-headed cowbirds (Molothrus ater), which decreases their breeding success. Northern yellow warblers have evolved defensive behaviours in response to cowbird visual and acoustic cues, but whether they use olfactory cues is unknown. My study addressed this research gap by testing how female cowbird odour impacts egg ejection and nest abandonment in these hosts. I applied preen oil from female cowbirds (threat odour) and female yellow-rumped warblers (Setophaga coronata, non-threat odour), and a no odour control to unparasitized yellow warbler nests during egg laying. I recorded host responses to these odours using trail cameras at the nest. Overall, nests treated with the threat and non-threat heterospecific odours elicited greater responsiveness to the area of treatment than controls. Hosts more frequently inspected the odour treated rim of the nest, oriented themselves toward the treatment location, and checked the status of their eggs. Although no instances of nest abandonment or egg ejection were observed, the increased behavioural responses to both heterospecific odours suggests that yellow warblers may be capable of recognizing foreign odour at the nest. These results provide evidence that olfactory cues may contribute information that the host can use in combination with visual and auditory to respond and defend against intruders at the nest.

section: Song and parental care: good dads sing simple songs
text:
Song and parental care: good dads sing simple songs
Presenter(s): Sarah Dobney1, Hayley Spina2, Ryan Norris3, Heather Williams4, Stephanie Doucet5, Daniel Mennill6
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Windsor, 2. University of Guelph, 3. University of Guelph, 4. Williams College, 5. University of Windsor, 6. University of Windsor
Session: Session 1: Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:40 UTC

Abstract
Elaborate bird songs are important for mate choice in many species. Song features may provide information about male parental behaviour or genetic quality. Using a field-based study of Savannah Sparrows in eastern Canada, we explored the relationship between male song and male parental behaviour. We measured male song rate and song structural features from audio recordings. We measured male provisioning rate from video recordings at nest sites. We found that male provisioning rate varied with song complexity: males who produced more introductory notes fed offspring less often. Given this relationship, we suggest that females may use male song to infer male parental behaviour when choosing a breeding partner. Upcoming genetic analysis of paternity will allow us to assess whether this relationship also influences genetic parentage. Investigating how male song features relate to parental care and female choice will improve our understanding of how reproductive behaviour is shaped by selection.

title: Presentations
section: Spatiotemporal variation in foraging behaviour and diet of breeding black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla)
text:
Spatiotemporal variation in foraging behaviour and diet of breeding black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla)
Presenter(s): Elora Edon1, Arnaud Tarroux2, Signe Christensen-Dalsgaard3, Manuel Ballesteros 4, Eeva Soininen5
Affiliation(s): 1. The Arctic University of Norway, UiT, 2. Norwegian Institute for Nature Research, 3. Norwegian Institute for Nature Research, 4. Norwegian Institute for Nature Research, 5. The Arctic University of Norway, Climate-ecological Observatory for Arctic Tundra
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 15:30 UTC

Abstract
Seabirds are experiencing global population declines, driven by multiple pressures including climate change and human activities. The black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla) is no exception to this trend and is currently classified as endangered on the Norwegian Red List. Therefore, understanding the patterns of seasonal distribution and foraging behaviour is a crucial step towards a better knowledge of the ecology and foraging strategies of this species. In this study, I explored the drivers shaping habitat selection in kittiwakes during the breeding season on Anda island, northern Norway. I used 12-year GPS tracking and reproductive rate data and combined them with information on diet based on 5 years of regurgitation samples collected from instrumented birds. The results showed that kittiwakes primarily used coastal habitats but relied on oceanic habitats as an alternative foraging habitat. Although the use of those two habitats varied substantially among years, kittiwakes appeared to track similar environmental niches rather than a fixed preferred habitat. However, greater reliance on oceanic habitats was associated with lower reproductive success, suggesting that increased use of distant offshore habitats may involve reproductive costs. Kittiwakes therefore appear to respond to a highly dynamic marine environment by adjusting their foraging behaviour. Taking this flexibility into consideration in conservation measures may help protect the habitats and prey resources needed to reduce further population decline.

title: Presentations
section: Spring Migration Strategies and Carryover Effects on Reproductive Success in Branta canadensis interior
text:
Spring Migration Strategies and Carryover Effects on Reproductive Success in Branta canadensis interior
Presenter(s): Laura Wallace1, Glen Brown2, Rodney Brook3
Affiliation(s): 1. Trent University, 2. Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources, 3. Ontario Ministry of Natural Resources
Session: Session 1: Migration
Time: 2026-10-06 19:20 UTC

Abstract
Arrival timing on breeding grounds is closely tied to reproductive success in migratory waterfowl. Better understanding of spring migration characteristics and carryover effects on annual productivity is needed to inform sustainable harvest management. Updated assessments of these population dynamics are notably important to guide harvest management decisions of the declining Southern Hudson Bay (SHB) population of Canada geese (Branta canadensis interior). Canada geese are the most harvested goose species across eastern North America, and SHB Canada geese are both culturally important and a key resource for subsistence hunters in Ontario’s northern communities. We investigated spring migration strategies of SHB Canada geese to assess how environmental conditions influence arrival timing and subsequent nesting success. From 2022–2025, we deployed 151 Ornitela GPS–GSM neck collar transmitters on adult breeding females, generating high-resolution movement data throughout the annual cycle. Using linear mixed effects models, we evaluated how snowmelt and temperature influence migration characteristics, and how those characteristics relate to nest success. Migration timing varied substantially among individuals, with arrivals to breeding areas ranging from mid-April to early May. Preliminary results indicate that regional snowmelt and temperature strongly influence the number and duration of migratory stopovers. Canada geese typically follow the snowline closely during spring migration, and some individuals arrived ahead of snowmelt and staged at lower latitudes until conditions improved. Importantly, later-arriving individuals exhibited lower nesting success, suggesting that delayed arrival may reduce reproductive performance. Our findings clarify spring migration strategies of the Southern Hudson Bay Population of Canada geese and highlight the importance of timely arrival for breeding success. Early arrival may benefit geese as spring phenology advances under climate change, yet mismatches between arrival timing and local environmental conditions could still affect productivity.

title: Presentations
section: Testing models of optimal caching: does intensity of feeder use change diurnal foraging patterns in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus)
text:
Testing models of optimal caching: does intensity of feeder use change diurnal foraging patterns in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus)
Presenter(s): Mechelle Goulart1, Ipshita Gayen2, Nathan Hobbs3, Kimberley Mathot4
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Alberta, 2. University of Alberta, 3. University of Alberta, 4. University of Alberta
Session: Session 2: Foraging Ecology and Diet
Time: 2026-10-06 16:50 UTC

Abstract
Many birds collect and store food for later use, called caching. Theoretical models predict that caching effort will be concentrated in a single peak during the day, though the precise timing of that peak depends on multiple factors. We studied diurnal patterns of feeder use in a population of 50 individually marked black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) in late summer. We used total daily feeder visits (1 visit ≈ 1 sunflower seed) as a proxy for caching intensity because daily feeder visits (range 11 – 339 feeder visits per bird per day) often exceeded required intake of about 45 sunflower seeds for chickadees at this time of year, consistent with a range of caching effort. Overall, chickadees exhibited bimodal foraging patterns. Further, we found that chickadees increased absolute feeder use throughout the entire day to accommodate increases in total daily feeder visits, as opposed to the single peak predicted by theoretical models of caching. Post-hoc analyses revealed that this population-level effect was driven by individual differences; some chickadees increased morning feeder visits with increasing total daily feeder visits, while others increased midday or end-of-day feeder visits. Future work should investigate drivers of these individual differences, including the role of interference competition.

title: Presentations
section: The Bird Who Cried Wolf: Hudsonian Whimbrels as Sentinel Alarm Callers in the Canadian Subarctic
text:
The Bird Who Cried Wolf: Hudsonian Whimbrels as Sentinel Alarm Callers in the Canadian Subarctic
Presenter(s): Mark Duchene1, Paul Smith2, Janet Ng3, Maggie MacPherson4, Erica Nol5
Affiliation(s): 1. Environmental and Life Sciences Graduate Program, Trent University, 2. Environment and Climate Change Canada, Ottawa, Ontario, 3. Environment and Climate Change Canada, Regina, Saskatchewan, 4. Department of Biology, Trent University, 5. Department of Biology, Trent University
Session: Session 2: Habitat Use and Breeding Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 19:30 UTC

Abstract
Aggressive behaviours, including alarm calling and predator mobbing, are frequently used by nesting birds to deter predators and improve reproductive success. These behaviours also provide opportunities for nearby nesting birds of other species to eavesdrop and glean information about predator threats, thereby reducing their nest predation risk. In the subarctic, whimbrels (Numenius spp.) frequently engage in aggressive alarm calling that may reduce nest predation risk and improve reproductive success of nearby nesting shorebirds. This has been suggested in Europe between Bar-tailed Godwits (Limosa lapponica) and Eurasian Whimbrels (N. phaeopus), where godwits choose their nest sites after whimbrels do and place them closer to whimbrels than expected by chance, possibly for protection. However, the influence of whimbrels on the incubation behaviour of nearby shorebirds has not been documented. Furthermore, nesting associations remain unexplored for other whimbrel species, such as the Hudsonian Whimbrel (N. hudsonicus) in North America. My research tests whether Hudsonian Whimbrel alarm calls affect the incubation behaviours of two co-occurring shorebirds, Short-billed Dowitchers (Limnodromus griseus) and Dunlins (Calidris alpina) in fen ecosystems near Churchill, Manitoba. To do so, I video-recorded incubating individuals during playback experiments featuring a randomized sequence of: 1) Hudsonian Whimbrel alarm calls, 2) Short-billed Dowitcher alarm calls, 3) Dunlin alarm calls, and 4) a sympatric frog chorus control (Boreal Chorus Frog, Pseudacris maculata; and Wood Frog, Lithobates sylvaticus), each separated by a 10-minute latency period. Fieldwork occurred in the summer of 2026, with results to be presented. As Hudsonian Whimbrels rapidly decline, this study may demonstrate their importance in shaping shorebird antipredator strategies and nest success in the Canadian subarctic. Doing so would provide justification to uplist their conservation status, consequently benefitting their entire shorebird nesting community.

text:
The Global Urban Bird Survey
Presenter(s): Paul J Preston1, Islamiat Abidemi Raji2, Daniel J Mennill3, Paul R Martin4, Lynn B Martin5, Alex M Syingi6, Massamba Thiam7, Guiherme Serpa8, Frances Bonier9
Affiliation(s): 1. Queen’s University, 2. Cornell University, 3. University of Windsor, 4. Queen’s University, 5. University of South Florida, 6. National Museum of Kenya, 7. Universite Cheikh Anta Diop, 8. Serpa Birding, 9. Queen’s University
Session: Session 1: Urban Ecology
Time: 2026-10-06 16:00 UTC

Abstract
Birds are a vital component of urban biodiversity worldwide, yet accurately measuring their abundance and diversity is challenging because most survey methods are not designed for dense urban environments. Surveys are often limited to green spaces, wealthier neighborhoods and high-income countries, hindering our understanding of how birds use all urban habitats. We developed and evaluated the Global Urban Bird Survey, an inclusive method for surveying urban birds across diverse city environments. Local experts trained and coordinated community members, who conducted repeated surveys using acoustic monitors in five cities between 2022 and 2024: Dakar, Nairobi, Rio de Janeiro, Paris, and Toronto. Survey locations were selected via a stratified block-randomized design within city cores, ensuring unbiased coverage across habitats. We compared the performance of the Global Urban Bird Survey with eBird, a widely used community science platform, to assess species richness, occurrence, and spatial coverage. eBird detected significantly higher mean species richness than the Global Urban Bird Survey in Dakar, Nairobi, Paris, and Rio de Janeiro, while no significant difference was observed in Toronto. However, eBird’s spatial coverage was substantially lower than that of the Global Urban Bird Survey, particularly in low-income cities. The Global Urban Bird Survey provides a robust, scalable approach to monitoring urban avian biodiversity across a range of habitats and socioeconomic contexts. Broader, more representative sampling of urban environments is critical for understanding global patterns of biodiversity. Community-based acoustic monitoring complements existing citizen science efforts, offering a tool for inclusive conservation planning and informed urban biodiversity management worldwide

section: The Road to Winter: Linking Departure, Settlement, and Selection in Greater Sage-Grouse
text:
The Road to Winter: Linking Departure, Settlement, and Selection in Greater Sage-Grouse
Presenter(s): Jordan Reynolds1, Dr Brad Fedy2
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Waterloo
Session: Session 1: Migration
Time: 2026-10-06 19:00 UTC

Abstract
Greater sage-grouse (Centrocercus urophasianus) winter habitat is typically delineated from where birds are found, treating occupancy as a single outcome rather than the product of nested decisions made at different scales. We decomposed overwintering into its components: when birds departed, where they could have settled, where they did settle, and what they used once settled. We tracked 43 greater sage-grouse in northeastern Wyoming from 2017 – 2022, defining each individual’s departure-to-settlement transition from net squared displacement changepoints rather than fixed calendar dates. Realized winter ranges were compared against potential ranges along each bird’s own trajectory, then against the broader study area (second order), and GPS fixes against availability within each bird’s range (third order), with collinear covariates screened a priori and candidate models ranked by AICc with k-fold cross-validation. Winter range placement was best explained by eastness, terrain ruggedness, topographic position, vegetation height, and sagebrush cover. Where greater sage-grouse avoided rugged terrain and selected for areas with higher vegetation cover and height (e.g., sagebrush and shrubs). Selection for taller, denser sagebrush at the scale of range placement suggests birds commit to areas where shrub structure is likely to remain exposed above snowpack across an entire winter, rather than locating such cover opportunistically once settled. Avoidance of rugged terrain is consistent with both the energetic cost of movement through snow and the tendency of broken terrain to accumulate drifts.

section: Thirty-seven years of change in an Arctic tundra bird community on Qikiqtaruk–Herschel Island, Yukon
text:
Thirty-seven years of change in an Arctic tundra bird community on Qikiqtaruk–Herschel Island, Yukon
Presenter(s): Maya Wade1, Isla Myers-Smith2, Cameron Eckert3, Richard Gordon4, Qikiqtaruk Territorial Park Rangers5
Affiliation(s): 1. University of British Columbia Faculty of Forestry & Environmental Stewardship, 2. University of British Columbia, 3. Yukon Parks, 4. Yukon Parks, 5. Yukon Parks
Session: Session 2: Conservation Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:40 UTC

Abstract
Climate warming is driving the expansion of woody shrubs across the Arctic tundra, reshaping habitats critical to over 200 bird species. Shrub expansion is already altering avian ranges, behaviours, and population dynamics, yet the magnitude of these effects and the diversity of species affected remain unclear. We examined whether the breeding bird community on Qikiqtaruk–Herschel Island, Yukon, has changed over the past 37 years and whether these changes are associated with increasing tundra greenness. Using 37 years (1990–2026) of annual June breeding bird surveys conducted by Yukon Parks, we tested for long-term changes in community composition using multivariate statistical analyses. We found that the tundra bird community composition shifted significantly and was largely driven by species turnover. Species richness and Shannon diversity exhibited small but significant positive trends over the study period. Several shrub-associated species such as American Tree Sparrow (Spizelloides arborea) and Bluethroat (Luscinia svecica) have increased, while many open-tundra-nesting species like Baird’s Sandpiper (Calidris bairdii) and Lapland Longspur (Calcarius lapponicus) have decreased. Environmental vector fitting identified maximum annual NDVI, a proxy for tundra greenness that reflects vegetation change such as shrub expansion, as the strongest predictor of these compositional shifts. These findings support the hypothesis that climate-driven vegetation change is contributing to the long-term restructuring of tundra bird communities, with potential consequences for the persistence of open-tundra specialist species.

section: Tracking nocturnal migration through flight calls: Insights from Motus Audio, a Canada-wide acoustic monitoring system
text:
Tracking nocturnal migration through flight calls: Insights from Motus Audio, a Canada-wide acoustic monitoring system
Presenter(s): Madison Bygrove1, Natalie Emerick2, Dan Mennill3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Windsor, 2. University of Windsor, 3. University of Windsor
Session: 3MT - Bioacoustics
Time: 2026-10-06 20:12 UTC

Abstract
Many migratory birds produce short nocturnal flight calls while traveling at night, providing species-specific acoustic signals that offer a powerful, non-invasive method for monitoring migration. Despite their growing use in migration research, the geographic and temporal patterns in flight call activity remain poorly understood. In this project, we investigate how nocturnal flight call activity in migratory birds varies among major flyways across Canada. We established a Canada-wide acoustic monitoring network—the Motus Audio Network—­comprising 100 custom-built autonomous recording units deployed across diverse habitats and migratory regions from coast to coast. We collected nightly recordings during spring and fall migration and identified flight calls using Nighthawk, a machine-learning algorithm that identifies nocturnal flight calls to the species or species-group level. The Motus Audio Network enables near-real-time monitoring of migration patterns across geographic scales that would be nearly impossible to achieve through traditional surveys alone. At 100 sites spanning from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland, we quantified the timing and magnitude of peak flight call activity during spring 2026 across four major migratory flyways. We predicted that each migratory flyway would show distinct peaks in migration timing, reflected by increases in flight call activity. Our research provides the first country-wide acoustic quantification of migration timing at a continental scale while providing species-specific insights into nocturnal migration. A deeper understanding of flight call patterns improves our ability to accurately predict migratory movements, identify high-risk areas, and inform conservation strategies aimed at reducing threats to nocturnally migrating birds in Canada.

section: Unforeseen effects of invasive birds on native birds after the simulated removal of mammalian nest predators in New Zealand
text:
Unforeseen effects of invasive birds on native birds after the simulated removal of mammalian nest predators in New Zealand
Presenter(s): Erin Bolger1, Paul Martin2, James Briskie3
Affiliation(s): 1. University of Saskatchewan, 2. Queen’s University, 3. University of Canterbury, Christchurch, New Zealand
Session: Session 2: Conservation Biology
Time: 2026-10-06 17:20 UTC

Abstract
Invasive predators are a major threat to native species on islands. Predator removal programs have been successfully implemented on many small islands to protect native species; however, the removal of invasive predators can have unforeseen negative effects on native species, mediated by other non-target invasive species. Identifying these indirect effects is important to maximize the effectiveness of predator removals. New Zealand is planning a country-wide predator removal program to conserve native species being threatened by invasive mammalian predators. However, predator removals are also expected to benefit invasive bird species that compete with native species. Life history data suggest the proliferation of invasive birds in response to island-wide predator removals, further endangering the native species. While previous localized predator removals in New Zealand suggested that the effects of invasive birds did not impact the success of predator removals for native birds, we found that on an island-wide scale, these effects are likely to be important. We tested for indirect effects from invasive birds on native birds using simulations that incorporated life-history and spatially explicit data, which allowed us to simulate the effects of different treatments on populations in a landscape. Our results suggest that island-wide predator removals will benefit native bird populations, but that these benefits are diminished by indirect effects mediated by invasive birds. Thus, we suggest that New Zealand plan to incorporate strategies to mitigate effects from invasive birds so that the success of the predator removal will be maximized for native species. Our simulation provides a modelling tool for predicting indirect interactions in an ecosystem and has the potential to be used as an invasive species management tool in the future.

text:
Using community science methods to assess predictors of urban avian species richness in Dakar, Senegal
Presenter(s): Lily Naaman1, Paul JE Preston2, Islamiat Abidemi Raji & Lab of Ornithology3, Cornell University4, Daniel J Mennill5, Paul R Martin6, Lynn B Martin7, Guiherme A Serpa8, Massamba Thiam9, Alex M Syingi10, Frances Bonier11

Department of Biology, University of Windsor, 5. Department of Biology, Queen’s University, 6. Department of Global Health, University of South Florida, 7. Serpa Birding, Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, 8. Universite Cheikh Anta Diop, Dakar, Senegal, 9. National Museum of Kenya, Nairobi, Kenya, 10. Department of Biology, Queen’s University
Session: 3MT - Citizen Science
Time: 2026-10-06 20:20 UTC

Abstract
Community science methods have the capacity to expand our knowledge of biodiversity by bridging barriers to research in economically marginalized regions, both globally and locally. The Global Urban Bird Survey (GUBS) collected audio and video recordings at randomized survey points distributed across the urban core of five cities around the world, including Dakar, Senegal. Although many studies have evaluated biodiversity in cities, primarily urban greenspaces, GUBS provides a more representative sample of avian species richness across all habitats in a city, providing important data on biodiversity in economically disadvantaged an underrepresented areas. We used the GUBS data from Dakar to assess relationships between green ground cover, human activity levels, and avian species richness, gauging the potential of using low-tech community science methods for these analyses. In addition to previously completed acoustic analysis to identify species richness at each survey point, we enlisted community members to rank green ground cover and human activity levels in 35 videos across the city of Dakar. We found that increased green ground cover and decreased human activity levels were associated with increased avian species richness. These preliminary findings provide evidence that predictors of bird biodiversity in Dakar city hold consistent patterns across diverse neighborhoods, even with the use of low-tech community science methods, paralleling previous evidence of positive effects of greenspace and negative effects of human activity on urban biodiversity. Given these findings, we are expanding the study to three of the other GUBS cities: Toronto (Canada), Nairobi (Kenya), and Rio de Janeiro (Brazil), to determine if the relationships we found in Dakar are consistent across these diverse cities. Overall, this study demonstrates the utility of low-tech approaches to evaluate the effects of features of the urban landscape that might limit or support biodiversity in cities.

text:
Vocal mimicry is widespread in tropical Seedeaters
Presenter(s): Nelsy Niño Rodríguez1, María Paula Sierra Oscar Laverde R2, Daniel J Mennill3
Affiliation(s): 1. Department of Biology, University of Windsor, 2. Departamento de Biología, Escuela de Ciencias e Ingeniería, Universidad del Rosario, Bogotá, Colombia, 3. Departamento de Biología, Facultad de Ciencias, Pontificia Universidad Javeriana Bogotá, Colombia, 4. Department of Biology, University of Windsor
Session: 3MT - Bioacoustics
Time: 2026-10-06 20:16 UTC

Abstract
Vocal mimicry occurs across diverse bird families, yet its ecological and evolutionary significance remains poorly understood. Although there are many well-documented examples of mimicry in temperate-zone birds, we know remarkably little about vocal mimicry in the tropics. The genus Sporophila comprises 41 species of small, seed-eating finches known as “Seedeaters”. To date, vocal mimicry has been reported in seven of these 41 species. Given the lack of detailed studies of the South American avifauna, we can anticipate that mimicry is more widespread and that many examples remain to be described. To assess the extent of vocal mimicry in the Sporophila genus, we retrieved sound recordings from two major sound libraries. We scanned all high-quality recordings to assess the presence of vocal mimicry and the percentage of recordings containing mimicry for each species. We mapped vocal mimicry onto a Thraupidae family phylogenetic hypothesis made from a time-calibrated global avian phylogeny. We pruned the tree to include all species of the Sporophila genus and six outgroup species to calibrate the tree. Our results reveal that mimicry is more widespread than previously recognized in this genus, suggesting an important role of vocal mimicry in this poorly studied genus.

Banding in the Age of Technology
Presenter(s): Marcel Gahbauer, Lesley Howes, Barbara Frei, Cyndi Smith, Pam Sinclair
Affiliation(s): Canadian Wildlife Service, Canadian Migration Monitoring Network
Organization Type: eNGO
Time: 2026-10-07 17:00 UTC

Abstract
Banding and recapture of birds in the early 1900s provided the first documentation of individual bird movements in North America. In recent decades, bird monitoring has been revolutionized by technological advances such as satellite telemetry, geolocators, and automated radio telemetry (e.g., Motus), as well as the growth of ‘big data’ through participatory science, and the use of artificial intelligence for species identification. This has prompted questions about whether traditional methods such as banding have become irrelevant. On the contrary, standardized banding efforts remain fundamental to understanding longevity, annual survival rates, age structure, and physiological responses to environmental change. Banding data also support a wide range of conservation and management outcomes, including disease surveillance and assessment of habitat restoration. Since 1998, the Canadian Migration Monitoring Network has facilitated communication and collaboration among bird observatories across the country. Maintaining strong banding programs while integrating emerging technologies is critical to advancing ornithological research and conservation.

Abstract
The Canadian Network of Avian Data (CanAvian) unites a broad community of researchers, conservation practitioners, and volunteer scientists who generate, manage, and share extensive biodiversity data needed for ecological research. CanAvian is governed by a Steering Committee, Advisory Committees, and Working Groups coordinating priorities across science, data management, and community engagement. CanAvian brings together three of Canada’s largest biodiversity data platforms: NatureCounts (380 million records), Motus (8 billion records), and WildTrax (16 million records), supporting over 4,500 scientific publications. Supported by the Digital Research Alliance of Canada, CanAvian is establishing harmonized data access policies and interoperability standards to support FAIR and CARE principles and improve data sharing across platforms and data repositories. These connections will support increasingly integrated and large-scale analyses required by modern ecological research and Canada’s biodiversity commitments. CanAvian has open pathways for membership, data contribution, and data access and invites participation from across Canada’s ornithological community.

Abstract
Birds Canada delivers strong science across the country and beyond through more than a dozen regional networks of employees, volunteers, and partners collaborating toward shared conservation goals. Our science is diverse involving many different research themes, core questions, methodologies, ecosystems, and focal species. Much of our science falls under two key initiatives: tracking the state of Canada’s birds and leveraging science to drive conservation. Our 50+ science staff members leverage data from volunteer scientists and conservation technologies (NatureCounts, Motus, WildTrax, and more) to answer timely questions of conservation interest, and we often partner with universities on graduate student projects. Ultimately all of our science helps generate the critical knowledge and evidence needed to catalyze actions that help birds and their habitats thrive. In this presentation, we give a top-down overview of science at Birds Canada, and describe a broad selection of examples of Birds Canada science in action.

Abstract
Parks Canada Agency monitors birds in protected areas across Canada within a common framework called the Ecological Integrity Monitoring Program (EIMP). This program assesses the status and trend of ecological integrity of 119 ecosystems within 43 national parks across the country and can enable prioritization and evaluation of management actions to enhance ecosystem integrity. Birds are one of the most common indicators, being monitored within six different ecosystem types in 39 parks. Of the avian indicators assessed in 2025, the proportion in good, fair and poor condition was 56%, 31%, and 11%, and the proportion improving, stable and declining was 11%, 43% and 19%. We provide a brief overview of the EIMP and a summary of bird indicators within the program. We also present a case study from a protected area to demonstrate how a monitoring indicator can be developed and used in the ecosystem management planning process.

Abstract
The Canadian Wildlife Service’s national wildlife management and assessment teams conduct research supporting the population monitoring and management of Canada’s migratory birds. Abstract
The Institute for Wetland and Waterfowl Research (IWWR) at Ducks Unlimited Canada conducts interdisciplinary research that advances ornithology within the broader context of wetland ecosystems. Centered on waterfowl ecology, IWWR studies waterfowl habitat use, productivity, and population dynamics, with particular emphasis on breeding landscapes such as the Prairie Pothole Region, while extending across boreal and other wetland systems nationally. Beyond core ornithological questions, IWWR develops quantitative tools and models to guide conservation planning and evaluate program outcomes, ensuring that habitat investments are effective, adaptive, and evidence-based. This includes assessing when programs should be refined, scaled, or phased out. Complementing our work in waterfowl ecology, we have developed substantial research capacity in biodiversity, climate change, carbon dynamics, wetland biogeochemistry, and sustainable agriculture, reflecting emerging priorities in wetland conservation science. Together, these efforts integrate waterfowl science with broader ecological processes to support both understanding and adaptive, outcome-driven conservation.

Twenty Years of Boreal Avian Modelling
Presenter(s): Elly Knight, Steven Van Wilgenburg, Diana Stralberg, Steve Cumming, Jeff Ball, Junior Tremblay, Erin Bayne
Affiliation(s): Boreal Avian Modelling Project
Organization Type: eNGO
Time: 2026-10-07 17:15 UTC

Abstract
The boreal forest is a vast and remote biome covering much of northern Canada and Alaska, which provides habitat for a substantial portion of the nearctic avifauna. The remoteness of much of this region limited earlier systematic monitoring efforts that hampered the development of data-informed decision support tools to aid bird conservation in response to increasing anthropogenic pressures. The Boreal Avian Modelling project (BAM) was formed as a collaborative initiative in 2004 to address this gap by amalgamating, harmonizing and integrating disparate point count data to develop tools for boreal bird conservation. We provide an overview of BAM’s development, including the individual research groups that make up the collective BAM team, and highlight BAM’s keystone tools for bird conservation. We discuss evolving conservation challenges and opportunities of new technologies and open data initiatives that can enhance science-based conservation tools for boreal birds.

Presenter(s): Tabatha Cormier (PhD Student), Nathanya Goudreau (MSc Student)

Organization Type: Academic

Abstract
Our research group, based at McGill University’s Macdonald Campus, investigates the link between avian movement, contaminants, physiology, and life history across many scales. Our study regions range from the Neotropics (Belize) to the Arctic (Hudson Bay), and many places in-between (Gulf of Alaska, St Lawrence system, Island of Montreal). In long-term collaboration with the McGill Bird Observatory, we investigate urban habitat use of migratory and resident songbirds around Montreal. We are also part of two long-term seabird monitoring programs at Middleton and Coats islands, where we work to understand the impacts of anthropogenic pressures on northern marine ecosystems. To answer our research questions, we combine biologging techniques (GPS, geolocators, accelerometry) and emerging technologies (drones, uncrewed surface vehicles), along with physiological biomarkers, contaminants, and doubly-labelled water experiments. Overall, our research informs management decisions and deepens our collective understanding of the natural world.
