title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Group living provides many potential benefits but can also incur important costs via competition for access to resources. Even in the absence of resource depletion, interference competition can reduce access to resources, and interference competition is not expected to affect all group members equally. In groups with dominance hierarchies, dominant individuals have priority access to resources and are therefore expected to experience lower costs of interference competition compared to subordinate individuals. We observed foraging behaviour in a population of 126 marked black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) at the University of Alberta Botanic Garden, near Edmonton, AB. We assessed the effect of manipulating the number of feeders available with ad libitum food on chickadee feeding territories, which we assumed would affect competition intensity, on total daily feeder visits. As predicted, we found strong evidence of interference competition: reducing feeder availability by 50% reduced average per capita daily visits to feeders in our population by circa 50%. Because chickadee flocks exhibit linear dominance hierarchies, with males being dominant over females, and at least in some populations, adults being dominant over immatures, we also investigated whether there was evidence for sex- and/or age-related differences in the strength of interference competition. We found that reductions in total daily feeder visits under lower manipulated food availability were similar for all age-sex categories, suggesting that females and immatures did not experience higher interference competition despite their subordinate status relative to males and adults. Post-hoc analyses revealed that adult females expanded their foraging area, while immature females increased both the length of their foraging window and their foraging area, when the availability of feeders was reduced. We suggest that these results may indicate that females invest more to mitigate competition and manage unpredictable access to food due to their subordinate status.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Estimating survival across different life-cycle stages is essential for contextualizing population patterns, developing species-specific conservation plans, and determining when data should be censored. This is particularly critical for migratory animals, such as waterfowl, as they experience diverse environmental conditions throughout their life. Capturing waterfowl for external transmitter attachment allows researchers to collect abundant movement and behavioural data across spatial and temporal gradients, but can expose birds to additional stress due to prolonged handling, sometimes leading to mortality. To determine if a data-censoring period is necessary and to understand the effects of the project’s capture and device attachment on mallard survival, we estimated the post-release survival of 1,263 tagged female mallards banded as part of the Eastern Mallard Project. We investigated the effects of individual bander, age, body mass, and temperature over a 15-day post-capture period using a Bayesian known-fate logistic exposure model. We found that mallards had a period survival rate of 0.97, with the greatest mortality during the first two days after capture and during extended exposure to cold temperatures, regardless of body mass or age. The majority of banders had negligible effects on daily survival, yet 12% had negative effects compared to the grand mean. We recommend that practitioners consider incorporating as few banders as feasible to deploy tracking devices for a given study design and spatial scale of deployments, because we anticipate that greater experience and consistency are easier to achieve with fewer people. Our results demonstrate the importance of contextualizing post-release survival in large tracking device projects, as environmental stressors and banding practices vary.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Incubating birds are expected to balance their energetic demands with thermal requirements of developing embryos. We explored whether clutch sizes were linked to nest attendance patterns in Red-breasted Mergansers (Mergus serrator), a sea duck in which conspecific brood parasitism is common, and females are solely responsible for incubation. We used nest temperature data to determine incubation period lengths, incubation constancy, and daily frequency and duration of incubation recesses by females at 15 successful nests. Maximum clutch sizes during incubation ranged from 6 to 19 eggs and the five largest clutches were parasitized by conspecifics. Clutch size was a poor predictor of incubation parameters, but mergansers initiating incubation later in the season had 3.6 d shorter incubation periods. We hypothesize that particularly warm nest temperatures later in the season (late July-early Aug) minimized daily variation in egg temperatures, thereby leading to shorter incubation periods for late-nesting females.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
ATP supply by mitochondria and ATP demand by cellular processes is carefully regulated during active periods and during states of metabolic suppression, such as torpor. Torpor is a state of inactivity characterized by decreased metabolic rate (MR) and body temperature that can be spontaneously reversed using endogenously produced heat. To avoid the high cost of thermoregulation at night, hummingbirds use torpor. We searched for a site of metabolic suppression in the flight muscle of torpid ruby-throated hummingbirds (Archilochus colubris). We were the first to investigate mitochondrial dynamics in hummingbirds. OXPHOS was suppressed by ~20% through CI when pyruvate was the metabolic fuel, but no suppression was observed when mitochondria were fueled with a lipid-based substrate. As fat is the main source of energy during torpor, we concluded that, unlike mammalian models of torpor, whole-animal MR suppression does not involve downregulating mitochondria. Next, we investigated ATP demand pathways to determine if inhibiting SERCA or Na+/K+ ATPase drives torpor. SERCA activity did not change, however, the uncoupler sarcolipin was more highly phosphorylated. Phosphorylation inhibits sarcolipin, resulting in decreased ATP demand and heat generation. Na+/K+ ATPase activity decreased by 43% in torpor, a mechanism that could account for a significant proportion of whole-animal MR suppression. Taken together, we suggest that torpid hummingbirds suppress pathways of ATP demand in concert with passive metabolic suppression initiated by adjusting thermoregulation and allowing core body temperature to drop. These findings highlight interesting contrasts between birds and mammals and provide insight into their evolutionary paths to heterothermy.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Song is a crucial aspect of sexual selection in songbirds, and is often an indicator of male quality. Song amplitude is a dynamic trait that birds can vary within and among songs. However, how song amplitude variation within songs reflects song quality has not been well examined. White-throated sparrow (Zonotrichia albicollis) genetic morphs (tan or white-striped) differ in their vocal behaviour but share the same two song types (up songs ascend in frequency between notes while down songs descend in frequency). Tan-striped males are preferred as mates yet sing less often than white-striped males. Thus, it is likely that differing structural components of song by morph may contribute to mate choice. Song amplitude has not been studied with respect to negative-assortative mating patterns in white-throated sparrows, nor has it been compared among up and down songs. We recorded song amplitude of white-throated sparrows using a field-portable recorder in Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, in the 2025 breeding season. We measured absolute amplitude of the whole song, as well as both absolute and relative amplitude of each note using bioacoustics software. We found that morphs did not differ significantly in absolute or relative amplitude of notes. However, we demonstrate that up songs increase in amplitude across the song, while down songs decrease in amplitude across the song. White-striped males singing up songs had higher mean and minimum song amplitude than those who sang down songs. Tan-striped males did not differ in amplitude for either song type. Our preliminary work suggests that song amplitude may be a feature that receivers could use to assess morph of mates or rivals.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Forest structural diversity has enabled the evolution and coexistence of diverse songbird communities in the boreal. Declines in many species have been tied to forest degradation, but we still lack a nuanced understanding of how fine scale habitat changes translate to landscape scale population impacts. Airborne laser scanning using LiDAR is quickly emerging as a tool for making this connection. Ontario has recently collected scans province-wide, using newly developed single-photon LiDAR (SPL) technology to produce a denser LiDAR dataset than is available elsewhere in Canada. Using a passive acoustic monitoring dataset from Mushkegowuk Cree territory in boreal northeast Ontario, I am completing the first multi-species test of SPL for wildlife habitat modelling. I predict that species-specific, niche-focused metrics derived from SPL data will allow more accurate species distribution modelling than has previously been possible, with some limitations imposed by lower canopy penetration of SPL than traditional LiDAR. For 91 study plots, I have calculated a set of standardized SPL habitat metrics across a range of spatial scales. By calculating single-species, single-metric response curves at each spatial scale for focal species with diverse habitat requirements, I have taken the first steps toward developing and testing niche-focused SPL metrics for boreal songbird modeling. Preliminary results show good predictive power of many test metrics for species using tree trunk and upper canopy niches, with species-specific differences in response to individual metrics that make biological sense. For shrub and forest floor associated species, few metrics have significant predictive power, but there still appear to be avenues for developing effective niche-focused metrics. This paves the way for comparisons of species distribution models using field data, basic SPL habitat metrics, and more refined niche-focused metrics.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Urban birds often incorporate anthropogenic materials into their nests. However, the factors that determine material selection remain unclear. Visual cues, such as colour, may influence birds’ choice of nesting material. European Starlings (Sturnus vulgaris), are a cavity-nesting songbird species observed to incorporate anthropogenic materials into their nests. Males build most of the nest as means to attract a mate and females help finish the construction. Although materials can be selected and added to nests, they can also later be thrown out rather than being further incorporated. This study investigates whether wild starlings exhibit a preference for certain colours of anthropogenic nesting materials. We provided birds with equal opportunity to select ribbons of five different colours (blue, gold, black, silver and white) and quantified both the colours selected from the environment and those incorporated into nests. Preliminary results indicate that certain colours are selected more often than others. Understanding the mechanisms underlying anthropogenic material selection in birds’ nests will improve our understanding of behavioural adaptations in urban environments and better inform conservation strategies.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Globally approximately 50% of woody plants rely on some form of animal mediated seed dispersal. Birds are one of the most important groups of seed dispersers due to their diversity in diet and their ability to move seeds. Movement of plants via birds has important implications for community structure and function as they can facilitate range expansions and genetic rescue for native and non-native plants. As landscape fragmentation increases and climate change advances, plant-bird interactions will have increasing significance for the adaption of plants. We are investigating the seed dispersal potential of Canadian migratory songbirds by comparing spring and fall movement of seeds, determining the potential for long distance dispersal of seeds by birds during migratory flights, and quantifying the viability of seeds dispersed by birds. We are using a combination of fecal samples collected from three migration monitoring stations in Ontario and Manitoba and stomach content analysis of window killed migratory birds collected by the Fatal Light Awareness Program in Toronto, to identify and quantify plant seeds carried by different bird species over the two migratory seasons. We assessed seed viability through tetrazolium and germination tests. Results to date indicate that 37% of fecal samples obtained from birds intercepted during migration at Long Point Bird Observatory in fall 2025, and 22% of stomach contents obtained from birds killed during fall and spring migration in Toronto 2024 contained plant seeds, including species in the genera Cornus, Juniperus, Parthenocissus, Rhamnus, Viburnum, and Vitis. Avian dispersers of plant seeds included Cedar Waxwing, Catharus thrushes, American Robin, Red-eyed Vireo, and White-throated Sparrow. These preliminary findings suggest that migratory birds may commonly move plant seeds during their migrations, shaping communities of native and non-native plants in Canada.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Playback is commonly used to survey birds, as it is an efficient method for censusing elusive species by increasing their detection probability. However, in Ontario Breeding Atlas surveys, playback surveys are not recommended. Then, Canada Warbler Cardellina canadensis (CAWA). Within our study region, Northwestern Ontario, this species has been historically understudied and underestimated due to low accessibility, but also because these birds are small, hard to see, and spend little time during the breeding season. However, CAWA is also known as a species that is attracted by social cues; previous studies suggested CAWA uses social cues (acoustic) for habitat choices. For these reasons, my hypothesis is that the use of playback songs/calls rather than only silent point counts will increase its detection. Through our experiment, we attempted to provide a valid insight into a more effective playback method for surveying our target species. During the breeding seasons of 2021, 2022, and 2023, I implemented a bird survey protocol using a silent period followed by playback song/calls and registered the detection of the species with and without the playback. I found that in about 70% of the cases, the bird was detected mainly after playing the songs/calls. In addition, I found that the species approached but were silent in unharvested areas, whereas in post-harvest areas they used to approach singing and/or respond with territorial calls. These results suggest that using playback protocols in bird surveys will increase the likelihood of Canada Warbler detections, especially in unharvested areas, leading to more accurate population estimates.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Agricultural ecosystems present complex trade-offs between human and conservation priorities, especially for migratory or at-risk species whose life cycles depend on managed habitats. Many avian species can provide valuable ecosystem services in agroecosystems, such as pest and weed control, yet these roles are often poorly quantified, especially during energetically demanding periods such as prior to migration. The Bobolink (Dolichonyx oryzivorus) is a long-distance migratory grassland passerine and species-at-risk with a distinct knowledge gap surrounding its dietary function within ecosystems, as well as its dietary patterns during pre-migratory staging. My study examines Bobolink diet during the post-breeding, pre-migratory staging period of July and August. I collected fecal samples across eight agricultural sites in the Annapolis Valley of Nova Scotia, Canada. Using DNA metabarcoding of fecal samples, I identified the dietary composition of plants and insects over time, between age groups, and in relation to plant origin and insect pest status. My results indicate that the Bobolink consumes a diverse dietary community of both plants and insects, including weeds and pests. This composition shifted significantly over time as migration approached, and insect dietary composition differed significantly between adults and juveniles. This study provides the first DNA metabarcoding analysis of the Bobolink, as well as the first fine-scale identification of the fall staging diet of the Bobolink. Together, these findings indicate that the Bobolink may contribute ecosystem services within agroecosystems while simultaneously shifting its diet to meet the energetic demands of migratory staging. By contributing to the knowledge of the Bobolink during a potentially limiting period of the life cycle, I hope to improve conservation management techniques by identifying important prey sources and emphasizing the value of this species-at-risk in agricultural ecosystems.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Many migratory birds produce short nocturnal flight calls while traveling at night, providing species-specific acoustic signals that offer a powerful, non-invasive method for monitoring migration. Despite their growing use in migration research, the geographic and temporal patterns in flight call activity remain poorly understood. In this project, we investigate how nocturnal flight call activity in migratory birds varies among major flyways across Canada. We established a Canada-wide acoustic monitoring network—the Motus Audio Network—­comprising 100 custom-built autonomous recording units deployed across diverse habitats and migratory regions from coast to coast. We collected nightly recordings during spring and fall migration and identified flight calls using Nighthawk, a machine-learning algorithm that identifies nocturnal flight calls to the species or species-group level. The Motus Audio Network enables near-real-time monitoring of migration patterns across geographic scales that would be nearly impossible to achieve through traditional surveys alone. At 100 sites spanning from Vancouver Island to Newfoundland, we quantified the timing and magnitude of peak flight call activity during spring 2026 across four major migratory flyways. We predicted that each migratory flyway would show distinct peaks in migration timing, reflected by increases in flight call activity. Our research provides the first country-wide acoustic quantification of migration timing at a continental scale while providing species-specific insights into nocturnal migration. A deeper understanding of flight call patterns improves our ability to accurately predict migratory movements, identify high-risk areas, and inform conservation strategies aimed at reducing threats to nocturnally migrating birds in Canada.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Temperate regions are known for their short, cool spring and summer during which birds breed and must forage intensely over days to provision their offspring. Such high levels of activities increase the heat generation, which the birds must effectively dissipate to maintain their activity. However, climate warming is projected to substantially increase temperatures during the breeding period, which may cause heat stress in birds and force them to reduce their activity and thereby negatively impact nestling quality. Currently, most studies measuring the avian mechanistic responses to heat stress are from arid and desert regions, while very few studies exist on those mechanisms in birds inhabiting colder regions. As climate change increases the likelihood of extreme heat events, avian responses to higher ambient temperatures must be studied in temperate regions. In this study, we aim to measure heat dissipation capacity of pine siskins (Spinus pinus), a small resident passerine distributed across North America. During autumn 2026, we plan to measure maximum thermal conductance and heat tolerance traits i.e. evaporative heat loss, resting metabolic rate, body temperature in captive siskins while exposing them to gradually increasing temperature in a metabolic chambers. Maximum thermal conductance (Cmax), which represents the highest capacity of the bird to dissipate heat without expending additional energy, will be calculated from the body temperature, ambient temperature, oxygen consumption and water vapor loss prior to the onset of panting. Once Cmax and maximum evaporative heat dissipation capacity are quantified, we can feed them into theorical model such as the Thermoregulatory polygon. This model will allow us to predict ambient temperatures which may cause heat stress and reduce nestling provisioning, which are crucial informations to understand the effects of climate warming on temperate birds.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Wildfire is a crucial primary disturbance in many forest ecosystems; however, anthropogenic climate change has increased its intensity, extent, and severity, drastically altering wildlife habitat and connectivity. These rapid and large-scale disturbances reduce habitat availability and impede dispersal pathways in the landscape. For forest-dependent species, it results in reduced gene flow, decreasing environmental fitness and adaptation. Black-capped Chickadee (Poecile atricapillus) is a resident forest species in North America, with limited dispersal and dependence on forest resources for survival, making it vulnerable to habitat fragmentation. Our study will focus on evaluating the genetic consequences of wildfire-driven habitat fragmentation in the Black-capped Chickadee by comparing genetic diversity, population connectivity, and levels of inbreeding pre- and post-fires. Our study will be conducted in central British Columbia (CBC), which has had a number of wildfire events in the last decade. We will be sampling five different sites relatively close to sites where samples were collected before the wildfire events, and genetically distinct populations were recorded. We will be using restriction-site associated DNA sequencing data to compare genetic patterns pre- and post-fires. Our study will provide a better understanding of how wildfire-induced habitat fragmentation impacts forest-dependent species population connectivity and will help inform targeted post-fire corridor restoration and conservation planning for forest-dependent species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Knowledge of reproductive attempts and outcomes is imperative for understanding drivers of population growth and learning how individual decisions and environmental conditions explain variation in productivity, but breeding locations in remote areas of the planet can hinder our ability to monitor reproductive attempts using traditional methods. The goal of this study was to develop a data-driven, machine-learning method that identified egg laying, incubation and brood rearing behaviour for two species of dabbling duck, American black ducks (Anas rubripes) and mallards (A. platyrhynchos), to measure reproductive success remotely using Global Positioning System (GPS) and tri-axial acceleration (ACC) data collected by tracking devices. We successfully developed an egg laying/early incubation model (classified as nesting or not), a full-term incubation model (non-incubating, failed incubation attempt or successful incubation attempt) and early (1-15 days post-hatch) and late (16-30 days post-hatch) brood rearing models (combined output as failed or fledged brood), which all had overall accuracies >94%. We applied our method to two large-scale datasets collected in eastern North America on black ducks and mallards and summarized data by species, age and year. We found mallards had greater breeding success than black ducks, due to higher nest propensity and brood fledging success. For each species, after second year females had higher nest propensity, nest success, and brood fledging success than second year females. Our method can be used to understand multiple fine-scale metrics of reproductive success using retrospective analysis of tracking data, should be applicable to most dabbling duck species, and could be adjusted for other taxa equipped with tracking devices that display restricted movements during breeding. Results from this approach allow hypothesis tests of environmental drivers of productivity and evaluations of their contributions to population change.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Longer-distance migrations by neotropical birds are expected to be associated with higher energy costs and lower survival, but may be compensated for by more food, longer daylengths, and fewer predators at more northern latitudes, resulting in higher productivity to offset the costs. However, there have been few empirical tests of these patterns and new conditions with climate change may limit the benefits of long-distance migration. We investigated the association between migration distance and nest productivity by using a rare, 30-year dataset (1995 – 2024) of over 100,000 nest monitoring records of the eastern subspecies of purple martin (Progne subis subis), spanning their entire North American breeding range (25–54° N). We analyzed the variation in clutch size and three measures of nest success across breeding latitude (where the most northern breeders migrate the furthest). We found strong latitudinal patterns of clutch size and nest success, where the most northern and southern breeders had the highest clutch sizes and fledged the most young, with intermediate latitudes showing lower productivity. Overall, these results contrast predictions that longer-distance migrations are compensated for by higher productivity at more northern latitudes. Further, regions with lower nest success in our study align with patterns of population decline in this species, suggesting a connection between productivity and population trends in this declining aerial insectivore. These findings overall highlight the importance of considering both spatial and temporal variation when determining the effects of migration distance on reproductive success and may help to explain steeper population declines in migratory songbirds.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Seabirds are experiencing global population declines, driven by multiple pressures including climate change and human activities. The black-legged kittiwake (Rissa tridactyla) is no exception to this trend and is currently classified as endangered on the Norwegian Red List. Therefore, understanding the patterns of seasonal distribution and foraging behaviour is a crucial step towards a better knowledge of the ecology and foraging strategies of this species. In this study, I explored the drivers shaping habitat selection in kittiwakes during the breeding season on Anda island, northern Norway. I used 12-year GPS tracking and reproductive rate data and combined them with information on diet based on 5 years of regurgitation samples collected from instrumented birds. The results showed that kittiwakes primarily used coastal habitats but relied on oceanic habitats as an alternative foraging habitat. Although the use of those two habitats varied substantially among years, kittiwakes appeared to track similar environmental niches rather than a fixed preferred habitat. However, greater reliance on oceanic habitats was associated with lower reproductive success, suggesting that increased use of distant offshore habitats may involve reproductive costs. Kittiwakes therefore appear to respond to a highly dynamic marine environment by adjusting their foraging behaviour. Taking this flexibility into consideration in conservation measures may help protect the habitats and prey resources needed to reduce further population decline.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Daily rhythms of light and dark regulate most biological processes and synchronize our internal physiology with the external environment. Artificial light at night (ALAN) has become a rapidly growing environmental pollutant, disrupting these rhythms. This disruption can adversely impact humans and wildlife, especially by disturbing the sleep-wake cycle, leading to cognitive implications that impact memory consolidation. Our research investigates the impact of ALAN on memory consolidation in black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus), a passerine songbird that relies heavily on spatial memory for winter survival. Previous studies have revealed that black-capped chickadees show what, where, and when memory. For my study, I manipulated the light-dark cycles and monitored the changes in their cognition by performing WWW memory tasks. Initially, the birds searched for sunflower seeds and mealworms in trees in an indoor aviary. Then these birds were allowed to revisit those sites after either short (3 hrs) or long (125 hrs) retention intervals, and their preference for food type was recorded. We hypothesized that birds would prefer mealworms during SRI and seeds during LRI, as the mealworms in LRI were degraded, and also higher light intensity will impair their WWW memory. Preliminary data showed that control birds preferred mealworms in their first four choices for both SRI and LRI, but this was not true for the other two treatments. Further data collection is needed to confirm these trends. By demonstrating that low-intensity light pollution can degrade sleep and memory in a diurnal species, this study highlights the need to reevaluate how artificial lighting affects the cognition and behaviour of wildlife.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Climate change is expected to alter habitat suitability and increase predation risk for the federally Threatened Hudsonian Godwit (Limosa haemastica) on their breeding grounds in the Hudson Bay Lowlands (HBL). Godwits have declined substantially in abundance over recent decades, but knowledge gaps regarding nesting requirements and habitat use limit conservation planning in Ontario. Our research aims to fill those gaps and investigate how variation in resource availability and predation risk on the landscape influences nest-site selection. As cryptic nesters, we expected Godwits to select for features that enhanced concealment and reduced predation risk; so, selecting for greater vegetation height, shrub cover, and distance from features like tundra ridges and trees. We collected high-resolution drone imagery covering a 70 m x 70 m area centered on fifteen Godwit nests in Polar Bear Provincial Park, Ontario from 2023 – 2025. Using that imagery, we generated land classification maps characterizing the habitat at each nest. We then tested for differences in habitat features and vegetation heights across spatial scales and between used (nest) and available sites. Findings revealed selection for nests with significantly taller vegetation within 1m2 compared to broader spatial scales and surrounding available habitat. Across all spatial scales, nests consistently featured dry graminoid fen, graminoid hummocks, and shrubs, and were rarely or never near exposed ground, flooded fen, water, trees, or ridges. Wet graminoid fen was selected against at the immediate nest site but included in the broader territory. Findings align with previous work on Alaskan and Manitoban breeding grounds, but contrastingly, no Godwits in this study nested near open water. Overall, this research provides insight into fine-scale nest-site selection by Hudsonian Godwits and suggests they may lose habitat suitability in the HBL as the boreal treeline expands northward into graminoid fen.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Many birds collect and store food for later use, called caching. Theoretical models predict that caching effort will be concentrated in a single peak during the day, though the precise timing of that peak depends on multiple factors. We studied diurnal patterns of feeder use in a population of 50 individually marked black-capped chickadees (Poecile atricapillus) in late summer. We used total daily feeder visits (1 visit ≈ 1 sunflower seed) as a proxy for caching intensity because daily feeder visits (range 11 – 339 feeder visits per bird per day) often exceeded required intake of about 45 sunflower seeds for chickadees at this time of year, consistent with a range of caching effort. Overall, chickadees exhibited bimodal foraging patterns. Further, we found that chickadees increased absolute feeder use throughout the entire day to accommodate increases in total daily feeder visits, as opposed to the single peak predicted by theoretical models of caching. Post-hoc analyses revealed that this population-level effect was driven by individual differences; some chickadees increased morning feeder visits with increasing total daily feeder visits, while others increased midday or end-of-day feeder visits. Future work should investigate drivers of these individual differences, including the role of interference competition.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Brood parasitism is when an individual lays their eggs in another’s nest, imposing the costs of raising those offspring on the parasitized individual (the host). In North America, northern yellow warblers (Setophaga aestiva) are frequently parasitized by brown-headed cowbirds (Molothrus ater), which decreases their breeding success. Northern yellow warblers have evolved defensive behaviours in response to cowbird visual and acoustic cues, but whether they use olfactory cues is unknown. My study addressed this research gap by testing how female cowbird odour impacts egg ejection and nest abandonment in these hosts. I applied preen oil from female cowbirds (threat odour) and female yellow-rumped warblers (Setophaga coronata, non-threat odour), and a no odour control to unparasitized yellow warbler nests during egg laying. I recorded host responses to these odours using trail cameras at the nest. Overall, nests treated with the threat and non-threat heterospecific odours elicited greater responsiveness to the area of treatment than controls. Hosts more frequently inspected the odour treated rim of the nest, oriented themselves toward the treatment location, and checked the status of their eggs. Although no instances of nest abandonment or egg ejection were observed, the increased behavioural responses to both heterospecific odours suggests that yellow warblers may be capable of recognizing foreign odour at the nest. These results provide evidence that olfactory cues may contribute information that the host can use in combination with visual and auditory to respond and defend against intruders at the nest.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Conventional definitions of boreal mixedwood forests are based solely on tree species composition, define species composition at a relatively coarse grain, and do not explicitly address spatial scale. Such definitions may oversimplify forest characteristics that are selected for by birds, potentially biasing past attempts to identify mixedwood habitat associations. To address this knowledge gap, we used a spatially-explicit approach to understand how three boreal bird species respond to continuous gradients in deciduous-coniferous composition, the spatial configuration of coniferous trees, and forest age within mixedwood forests in Alberta, Canada. We used a boosted regression tree model to assess the influence of these habitat characteristics across multiple spatial extents (150 m, 500 m, 1000 m) and grain sizes (5 m and 30 m) on bird relative abundance. Spatial configuration was the strongest predictor for all three species. Black-throated green warbler (Setophaga virens) and bay-breasted warbler (Setophaga castanea) responded most strongly to fine-grain, local (150 m) configuration, with abundance peaking in intimately mixed stands. Tennessee warbler (Leiothlypis peregrina) responded most strongly to configuration at the broadest extent (1000 m), also favoring intimate mixtures. The proportion of conifer and forest age consistently emerged as the second and third most important predictors, respectively. Predicted abundance on synthetic landscapes showed consistently higher abundance (~ 4-10 times higher) in intimate versus segregated mixedwoods. Our results demonstrate that species-specific and spatially-explicit mixedwood definitions that include conifer spatial configuration better capture bird habitat use than composition alone. Preserving or restoring intimate mixtures of coniferous and deciduous tree species at fine spatial scales may be particularly beneficial for our focal species.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
An ecological trap occurs when an animal shows a preference for a habitat that ultimately has negative fitness consequences. Birds nesting in urban areas may be particularly vulnerable to ecological traps. Alternatively, some parts of urban areas may act as shields, when human presence function as a deterrent to some common nest predators. Open-cup, ground-nesting birds are considered susceptible to disturbance from human recreation and predation by urban predators. Urban breeding Spotted Towhees (Pipilo maculatus) often nest in dense and shrubby habitat along edges, thus are a good study system to test for ecological traps. In urban areas, these edges often border walkways which may alter disturbance or predation risk due to human activity. From 2022-2025 we found and monitored 407 Spotted Towhee nests across five greenspaces of varying degree of urbanization within Metro Vancouver, British Columbia. We examined how daily nest survival and reproductive success are impacted by natural and anthropogenic factors across multiple spatial scales ranging from the level of nest sites to the entire urban greenspace. We also tested whether nesting decisions of Spotted Towhees breeding in urban greenspaces create an ecological trap or provide a shield from predation. We found that nest survival and the number of fledglings produced were both affected by weather and probability of nest survival increased with increasing degree of urbanization. We showed that Spotted Towhees preferably nest close to anthropogenic edges, like paths, but found that these edges are not functioning as a trap for towhees during the nesting stage because the distance to edge did not significantly impact nest survival or number of fledglings produced. Our findings support the hypothesis that human dominated environments benefit some native species, potentially through a shield phenomenon, highlighting the potential role urban environments can have for bird conservation.

title: SCO-SOC Virtual Meeting 2026
text:
Abstract
Urban habitats offer many unique opportunities and challenges to various bird species. With the global land-cover of cities expected to double over the next 25 years, it is crucial to understand how birds are surviving and moving in urban landscapes. Past research on urban settings has focused on the survival and reproductive success of breeding birds. There is significantly less research into the movement and survival of songbirds overwintering in urban areas. This discrepancy is important as many species spend large portions of their life-cycle in there wintering ranges, and this may also be the time when food and predation pressures are at there highest. We studied how Golden-crowned sparrow Zonotrichia atricapilla movement and survival differs from rural parks to urban neighborhoods in Metro-Vancouver. 30 birds were radio-tagged across five sites in the winter of 2025-2026, and an additional 200+ birds were colour-banded across six sites from 2021-2026. We tracked the radio-tagged birds for six weeks to obtain details on fine-scale movements to determine habitat use and home range size, and to ascertain known-fate survival. Reported colour-band resightings were used to estimate broad overwintering Golden-crowned sparrow apparent-survival. We found that areas of increased urbanization had lower rates of known-fate survival and higher rates of unexplained disappearances. Birds initially caught in the proximity of static bird feeders had smaller home ranges than the home ranges of birds that were not caught in close proximity to feeders. Through colour-band resightings, we found that birds overwintering in areas with higher rates of urbanization had lower rates of apparent-survival than those living in rural areas. These findings indicate that while urban habitats are suitable for overwintering Golden-crowned sparrows, these benefits are mitigated by potential survival risks, and more research is needed to understand the mechanics of these relationships.

Abstract
Seabirds are central place foragers, and can be good indicators of prey distribution in regions such as the Arctic, where direct monitoring of prey is challenging. However, different species of seabirds make specific foraging decisions based on different combinations of factors. For example, in selecting forage locations, common murres have been observed to use both memory (foraging at sites with persistent prey) and local enhancement (foraging where conspecifics are feeding) more than information exchange at the colony. Since forage site characteristics versus colony characteristics are key for common murre foraging choice, our study focussed on at-sea factors potentially affecting foraging seabirds. We monitored thick-billed murres (Uria lomvia) and their prey at and around two Canadian Arctic islands that support different sized thick-billed murre colonies. We attached biologgers to murres’ lower back or tail feathers at the nesting sites and deployed a remotely-monitored, uncrewed sailing vessel (Sailbuoy) equipped with an echosounder to record prey presence along the Sailbuoy’s route. By overlaying GPS-linked accelerometry and hydroacoustic data collected over the same time period, we were able to test the match between thick-billed murres’ foraging effort and the spatial persistence of prey over the breeding season. This information will allow for real world comparison of seabird foraging routes and prey distribution, and reveal more about which factors affect how to use seabirds as indicators to assess the stability of ecosystems that are difficult to monitor directly.
